Issue 8, continued: the lifecycle replay, agreed. The next release moves the IPC schema to 12, so the newest release of another schema is v0.29.0. Its daemon, idle and drained at schema 11 as the new client drains one, was still there 6.3 s later, draining with no job, and a run was refused daemon_draining (exit 112); its own client's daemon stop --grace, which waits for no job and then stops, ended it in 0.1 s. Under issues 4 and 5 a replay against it would wait without end on --grace and refuse its run after daemon.start-timeout. run --exercise through a daemon to 192.0.2.1 with the replay's credentials exited 0, device_contacted: false, no ssh process started. The rule. Nothing is done for a daemon from before this chapter (at the operator's word: no one runs one, and the next client never reaches its daemon.sock), and issues 4 and 5 stand. The next release has no lifecycle replay: at that release common.sh's PRIOR_VERSION is emptied, its comment saying why, v0.29.0's daemon predating the drain that exits and listening on daemon.sock; evidence-rest.sh's skip line names common.sh for the reason, no longer saying that no release's schema differs; and BUILD-QUALIFICATION's history of priors says there was none for it. In the build the replay moves to this rule: the status read by its stacked keys; its run step run --exercise to 192.0.2.1, the idle older daemon drained, exiting, and replaced by the client's; and --grace and --after draining first. Its first run is at the release that next moves the schema, against the next release. Not taken: the wait after a drain ending at no job and stopping a daemon still answering, and a daemon's missing commit and build shown none (each for a past release's daemon alone); the replay run in the build against a lab build at another schema.

Issue 9, the documents, agreed. The documents that say what this chapter changes, found by their words (compatible, daemon restart, --grace, drain, daemon_incompatible, build_time, Restart=, upgrad): DESIGN sections 7, 8, and 16; OPERATIONS' "Upgrade" and "The daemon's idle exit"; QUICKSTART's "After upgrading from an older daemon"; ARCHITECTURE's "Daemon upgrade boundary"; README's "Release status"; BUILD-HOWTO sections 4.2, 4.3, and 8; BUILDING; BUILD-QUALIFICATION; the manual page karvi-daemon(1), its DESCRIPTION generated from the help and its FILES written by hand; ERROR-CODES and the reference, generated from their registries; examples/config.toml; the packaged unit; FILES section 4.7; the CHANGELOG; and the ROADMAP. Found: README's counters line and BUILD-HOWTO section 8 name the configuration registry 28, the tree at 29 since daemon.sockets, which daemon.launch does not move again (the counter moves once a release); and BUILD-QUALIFICATION's daemon upgrade gates require a run beside the schema-2 fixture to fail with exit 112 and start no daemon, where under this chapter the run drains an older daemon. The rule. The documents say what this chapter builds, and nothing of a daemon from before it. The generated ones move with their code in each section of the build, make generated-clean holding at every commit: ERROR-CODES (build_unreadable and daemon_other_build new; daemon_incompatible a newer schema, or a unit's daemon of another build; daemon_draining the client's own drain of a busy daemon as well; daemon_stop_wait_interrupted the daemon finishing its jobs and exiting, no longer remaining draining); the reference and the configuration schema (daemon.launch, its documentation naming the centralized install); and karvi-daemon(1)'s SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION from the help.

The written ones come in the build's closing section, one commit, then make html. DESIGN: section 8's entry replaced by "A daemon serves its own build; a client drains another's" (the rule, issues 5 and 6; its Why that nothing is killed, the drain finishing the jobs); "daemon stop and daemon restart refuse an active daemon without an option" amended by issue 4's --grace, --after, and interrupt, and "job follow renders the whole job as the foreground run would have" by issue 6; new entries, "A drained daemon exits after its last job" (issue 4) and "A unit's daemon is its administrator's" (issue 7) in section 8, "A build is its Go build ID's last part" (issues 1 and 2) and "The client judges the daemon; the daemon checks nothing of the client's" (issue 3) in section 7, and "A build is stamped with its version and its commit" (issue 8) in section 16; "Shutdown is a cause, not a cancel" and "The daemon leaves by itself when idle" unchanged. OPERATIONS: "Upgrade" rewritten for the operator's own daemon, with nothing to run: the next submission drains a daemon of another build, an idle one replaced in the same invocation (daemon drained …, daemon started …), a busy one refused with the builds stacked until its jobs end, --no-daemon meanwhile, and job follow and job cancel reaching its jobs; daemon status's pairs; daemon stop --grace to end it; an older karvi beside a newer daemon refused, karvi daemon stop from the newer; the v0.10.0 preview's paragraph removed. A new section after "The daemon's idle exit", "A service account's daemon under its unit": the centralized install (the service account, loginctl enable-linger, the packaged user unit installed for it, daemon.launch = false in its configuration or locked in the site's global file, the administrator's systemctl --user restart after an install), TimeoutStopSec=infinity and the grace keys, a client of another build refused naming the unit, daemon stop and restart refused naming systemctl, unit: in daemon status, and no other UID reaching the daemon; "The daemon's idle exit"'s unit paragraph points to it. QUICKSTART's section becomes "After an upgrade", two sentences and karvi daemon status. ARCHITECTURE's "Daemon upgrade boundary" rewritten: the build read from /proc/self/exe; the probe at the lifecycle envelope, the schema and then the build; ensureDaemon's sequence; the drain at the daemon's schema; follow and cancel at the schema alone; the prepare answer's daemon block checked; INVOCATION_ID and daemon.launch. README: "Release status"'s compatibility sentence and its paragraph "A newer client still inspects, stops, and restarts a daemon launched by an older executable" replaced by the rule; the counters line (registry 29, IPC 12, plan 13) and the reproduction command (issue 8). BUILD-HOWTO: section 4.2's command; section 4.3 pointing to the install method; section 8 rewritten as OPERATIONS' "Upgrade" in short, with the counters. BUILDING: the command, and its sentence on COMMIT, no BUILD_TIME and the default from git. BUILD-QUALIFICATION: the commands; the verifiers' check of the build; the daemon upgrade gates rewritten for the rule, the fixture answering a drain by exiting as a daemon of this chapter does (built with the suite). karvi-daemon(1)'s FILES: the drained daemon's exit, and the unit's paragraph (TimeoutStopSec=infinity, daemon.launch, the administrator's restart). examples/config.toml: a commented [daemon] table with launch = false and its reason. The packaged unit: TimeoutStopSec=infinity with its comment, and a comment naming daemon.launch and the restart after an install. FILES section 4.7: the units' row pointing to OPERATIONS' new section. The CHANGELOG's ## Unreleased, the breaking changes first: a daemon serves its own build, a client draining another's; daemon status's keys renamed, text and JSON; IPC 12 and plan 13; a drained daemon exiting, and --grace and --after draining any daemon; the unit; karvi version's build: and no build_time, and make build's commit from git; then follow and cancel across builds, job_orphaned's fix, and the new codes. The ROADMAP: Next 1 removed once built, the next item the operator's, asked at the build's end. At the release, not before: BUILD-RESULT.md and release-manifest.json name the build, common.sh's prior emptied, and BUILD-QUALIFICATION's history of priors gains the release (issue 8).

Issue 10, found while building S3: the stop's mode, its count, and the wait, agreed. On the lab build of section 3, during a 30-second job, a stop naming if_idle was refused, daemon_active_jobs, and one naming no mode was answered stopping: the run lost its follow at 5.1 s (follow_stream_lost, exit 111), and the daemon left at 10.1 s logging shutdown_incomplete, the job's folder without its summary. The client named the mode only to a daemon it judged compatible, of its schema and version and, since section 1, its build, so a build of section 2 beside the section's daemon sent daemon stop --force with none: daemon_stop_timeout (exit 106) after 10 s and the job lost so, where a build of section 3 had it recorded incomplete_shutdown (exit 106) with its summary. With no option that client counted the daemon's jobs itself, from its probe, which no job another client submits before the stop reaches. A drained daemon stopped with --force logged stopping: drained as its cancelled job ended, and one sent SIGTERM after a drain logged the signal's stop and the drain's. --grace's client waited without a word; ended by SIGINT or SIGTERM (exit 113, its message), SIGHUP (129), or SIGKILL (137), it left the drained daemon to finish its job and exit; and an --after=5s interrupted at 1 s forced nothing at 5 s. The rule. Every stop and restart the client sends names its mode, if_idle without an option and force under --force and at --after's limit, and the client counts nothing: the daemon alone counts its jobs, under the lock that admits them, so that no job is admitted between the count and the stop; it refuses an if_idle stop while any run and takes a stop that names no mode as if_idle; --grace, --after, and --force overrule the refusal (at the operator's word, no daemon of an older release considered). A stop or a signal after a drain takes over from it, so that the log names the stop that ended the daemon. A --grace or --after wait on a daemon with jobs begins with a line on standard error, the jobs from the drain's answer and an earlier drain from the probe's status, every time, so that an operator back after a broken wait is told; --quiet leaves it out:

daemon draining: 1 job running; waiting for it to exit
daemon already draining: 2 jobs running; waiting for it to exit
daemon draining: 1 job running; waiting up to 5s, then forcing

Not taken: the client's count before the stop (blind to other clients, the daemon's needed anyway); a stop naming no mode stopping at once (its jobs lost unrecorded); the daemon holding --after's limit, so that it outlives the client (at the operator's word, the wait and its limit are the client's).

Issue 11, found while building S3: the grace and systemd's stop limits, agreed. This host's systemd 259 (Ubuntu) stops a login session's scope, where a client-launched daemon runs, in 90 s, KillMode=control-group, and user@.service, the user manager under which a user unit runs, in 5 s, by the package's drop-in user@.service.d/timeout.conf, KillMode=mixed; read from the configuration, no shutdown run. At a shutdown a daemon receives SIGTERM, drains, every new job refused (daemon_draining), and waits daemon.shutdown-grace-seconds, 120 by default, for its jobs before cancelling and recording them: the scope's 90 s killed it first. Scaled on transient user scopes with TimeoutStopSec=5, a 30-second job stopped with the scope: under a grace of 3 the job was recorded incomplete (exit 106) with its summary and the socket removed; under a grace of 8 the daemon was killed at 5.2 s, the run losing its follow (exit 111), the job without its summary and the socket left. The rule. daemon.shutdown-grace-seconds defaults to 60, under a session's 90 s, its registry text saying why, and the planner's pinned draft digest moves with it. A user unit's 5 s, which the unit's TimeoutStopSec=infinity cannot lengthen, is issue 7's, opened for section 5's design.

Issue 12, found while building S4: what issues 5 and 6 left unsaid, agreed. On the lab of section 4, A and B two builds of the tree and N the tree at 0.30.0 and IPC schema 13: B's run beside A's idle daemon drained it and started B's in the same invocation, exit 0; beside A running a job it was refused, daemon_draining (exit 112), and so was A's own run, A exiting by itself at its job's end; N drained and replaced B's idle daemon, of an older schema to N; and B beside N's daemon was refused. Four things the issues did not say were settled in the build. The rule. A drained daemon holding no job that has not exited within daemon.start-timeout refuses the submission in issue 5's layout (in the unit test: a daemon exits within milliseconds):

daemon_draining: no job running, not exited after 5s; none submitted; karvi daemon stop, or --no-daemon
  daemon build 9Au3WHU839F5xE-67H93 0.29.0
  client build XfTtoeK1qq9HkGakcVu7 0.29.0

A daemon of a newer IPC schema, whose build the client cannot read, is refused with the schemas stacked as the builds are, and job follow and job cancel beside a daemon of another schema name the karvi that speaks it, an older daemon's by the version it answered with, a newer one's as the newer karvi:

daemon_incompatible: the daemon speaks a newer IPC schema; none submitted; karvi daemon stop from the newer karvi, or --no-daemon
  daemon ipc_schema 13
  client ipc_schema 12
daemon_incompatible: the daemon speaks an older IPC schema; follow its jobs with karvi 0.29.0
  daemon ipc_schema 12
  client ipc_schema 13

The dry run's daemon line and the exercise report's name the daemon's build after its version, so that daemon_other_build's finding is read against it: daemon local: incompatible pid=… version=0.29.0 build=XvVcKUyDY-UJ1l3tZw8E ipc_schema=12. An interrupt during the sequence's wait, for a drained daemon to exit or a launched one to answer, is cancelled (exit 113), nothing having been submitted, where it was daemon_start_failed (112). A daemon of another build that prepares the job a second time, after the sequence has run once more, is refused daemon_incompatible, its registry text saying so. Not taken: the client stopping a drained daemon that has not exited (a client drains and never stops); the schemas on one line (two values compared are read stacked); the client's build on the dry run's line (karvi version names it); a code of its own for the second prepare (three daemons in one invocation, the code that names a daemon the client will not use).

Issue 13, found while designing section 5: the unit's kill mode, agreed. The packaged unit names no KillMode, so systemd's control-group applies: a stop sends SIGTERM to every process of the unit at once, the daemon and each OpenSSH process of the system transport. On a transient user service with TimeoutStopSec=infinity, as issue 7 has the unit, a 12-second job (sleep 12; echo done) through the system transport to 127.0.0.1 and the unit stopped 3 s into it: under control-group the stop returned at 3.1 s, the job's session lost (command_session_lost, exit 101, its summary errored); under KillMode=mixed, SIGTERM to the daemon alone and SIGKILL to what remains once it has exited, the job ran to its end, exit 0, completed, the stop returning at 12.3 s; under mixed with a grace of 4 the daemon cancelled and recorded it at 7.1 s, incomplete_shutdown (exit 106), nothing left in the unit's cgroup. A job of the native transport has no child and drained under either, as on issue 7's lab. The rule. The packaged daemon unit sets KillMode=mixed beside TimeoutStopSec=infinity: a stop or a restart signals the daemon alone, which drains and ends its own sessions within its grace, and systemd kills what remains after it exits; the unit's comment says so. A login session's scope, where a client-launched daemon runs, stops by control-group too, so at a shutdown, or a logout that ends the user's processes, that daemon's jobs of the system transport end at once, recorded as on the service; no unit of karvi's sets that scope. Not taken: control-group (every OpenSSH session cut with the daemon's SIGTERM, the drain defeated for the system transport); process (the daemon alone signalled, and what it leaves keeps running after it).

Issue 14, the service account's daemon at a host's shutdown, agreed. Issue 11 found a user unit's daemon under user@.service's 5-second stop at a shutdown, which the unit's TimeoutStopSec=infinity cannot lengthen. With netops.test standing for the service account, a 12-second job on the fake device, and the stop 3 s into it. A user unit (TimeoutStopSec=infinity, KillMode=mixed) under the account's user manager, the manager stopped as a shutdown stops it: the daemon killed 5 s later, the run losing its follow (follow_stream_lost, exit 111), the job without its summary, d.sock left. The same with a drop-in for that account's manager alone raising its stop to 90 s: the job completed, exit 0; but a drop-in named karvi-s5.conf sorted before Ubuntu's timeout.conf, which won, and the stop stayed 5 s, where one of the same name or sorting after it took. A transient system unit, User=netops.test, TimeoutStopSec=infinity, KillMode=mixed, Wants= and After=network-online.target, no user manager and no linger: the stop waited, and the job completed, exit 0, at 12.7 s. network-online.target is loaded and active in the system manager and not-found in a user manager, so the packaged user unit's After= ordered nothing. Found: logind's RemoveIPC=yes, the default, removes every file an account owns under /dev/shm 10 s (UserStopDelaySec) after its last logind session ends, a user manager started for it counting as one: a first run of the system unit's case lost its running job's manifest and commands.jsonl so, the job ending errored. System users are excluded (logind.conf(5)), a lingering user is never finalized, and sudo -u opens no session. The rule. A service account's daemon runs under a system unit: the package ships the template karvi-daemon@.service, User=%i, which the administrator enables for the account, systemctl enable --now karvi-daemon@ACCOUNT.service, started after the network, stopped at a shutdown before the network goes, and bounded by the daemon's grace alone (TimeoutStopSec=infinity, KillMode=mixed), with Restart=on-failure and the idle timer off as before, and no user manager or linger. The account is a system user (adduser --system), whose files logind leaves alone. The packaged user unit karvi-daemon.service is removed. Issue 7's words move with it: no loginctl enable-linger and no systemctl --user; daemon status names unit: karvi-daemon@ACCOUNT.service; daemon stop and daemon restart refuse naming systemctl restart of that unit; and the crun unit's comment names the template. An operator's own daemon is the client's launch (issues 1 to 6); an operator who kept one through a logout under the user unit on a host that ends users' processes at logout no longer can. Not taken: the user unit as issue 7 had it (killed 5 s into every shutdown on Ubuntu); the user unit with a drop-in for the account's user manager (three things to set, a drop-in's name that loses without a word, and no order against the network); a packaged drop-in for every user's manager (every user's shutdown changed). Noted, not opened: an operator's own daemon running after the operator's last logout loses the operator's files under /dev/shm, the scoreboards among them, 10 s later.

Issue 15, how a client knows a daemon is systemd's, agreed. Issue 7 has a client never drain a unit's daemon: drained, the daemon exits 0, which Restart=on-failure does not restart, so after an install the account's first run would leave it without a daemon until the administrator acted. Neither the daemon's pid nor its parent tells who started it: a client's launch from a login session has PID 1 for its parent, as a system unit's daemon has, and a client's launch from a user service's shell the user manager, as a user unit's daemon has. The daemon's environment and cgroup would tell it (INVOCATION_ID set and the cgroup ending in the unit's .service, where a client's launch, which filters the environment, has no INVOCATION_ID), at the price of the daemon reading both and its answer naming its unit and its manager. The client's own configuration says it more plainly. The rule. daemon.launch names who starts the account's daemon, a word, as display.color takes one: "client", the default, the client starting its own daemon as issues 1 to 6 have it, for an operator; "systemd", set for the service account by the install script, or locked for every operator of a host in the site's global file, the daemon started by the unit karvi-daemon@USER.service, USER the client's own account. Under "systemd" a client sends no drain and starts no daemon: a daemon of its own build not draining takes the submission; a daemon of another build refuses it, never drained, in issue 5's layout:

daemon_incompatible: the daemon runs another build; none submitted; systemctl restart karvi-daemon@karvi.service, or --no-daemon
  daemon build 9Au3WHU839F5xE-67H93 0.29.0
  client build XfTtoeK1qq9HkGakcVu7 0.29.0

A draining daemon, stopping under its unit, refuses it daemon_draining as in issue 5; with no daemon the submission and daemon start are refused daemon_unreachable, naming systemctl start of the unit; daemon stop and daemon restart are refused with a new code, daemon_managed:

daemon_managed: daemon.launch is systemd; systemctl stop karvi-daemon@karvi.service

The dry run reports a daemon of another build as an error, and daemon status's remediation names the unit's restart. The daemon is unchanged: it names no unit and reads neither its environment nor its cgroup, which replaces issue 7's unit: line, its INVOCATION_ID, and its boolean daemon.launch. Not taken: the daemon knowing its unit from INVOCATION_ID and its cgroup (a reading and two fields where the client's setting says it); the parent pid (above); daemon.launch a boolean (false says what a client does not do, not who does); "systemd-managed" (the key already says launch); the refusals naming "its unit" (the install script enables exactly karvi-daemon@USER.service).

Issue 16, the service account's install and its removal, agreed. What it gains: the service account's daemon under systemd set up on a host in one command, run as root, and undone in one, where OPERATIONS would otherwise give the administrator steps to follow and to remember for their undoing. It waits on issues 14 and 15, the template unit and daemon.launch = "systemd", and is built with them. Found while designing it: a home at /var/lib/karvi, one of karvi's two system roots, owned by the account at 0700, would refuse other operators' runs, which look for /var/lib/karvi/shared and /var/lib/karvi/users/<username> there and pass by an absent one but not one they may not read (internal/osutil/paths.go, read, not run). The rule. A bash script, karvi-sysutil, in the tree's packaging/sbin/ and installed as /usr/sbin/karvi-sysutil with a manual page karvi-sysutil(8), its commands naming their object as karvi's do: sudo karvi-sysutil daemon install [--group NAME] and sudo karvi-sysutil daemon remove [--purge]. It runs as root alone, directly or through sudo, and exits 1 otherwise. daemon install, in order: runs karvi setup shared --group NAME, which reports each place exists on a host already set up, so that the site's shared trees and /opt/karvi/users exist, every operator's jobs, collections, and transcripts then going to the trees under /opt/karvi/shared; makes the account karvi, a system user (issue 14) with its group, its home /opt/karvi/users/karvi, which is also its private root, and no login shell, an existing account of that name taken only when it is a system user; adds it to the operators' group, netops unless --group names another, a group that does not exist refused; writes the account's /opt/karvi/users/karvi/.config/karvi/config.toml, its own and mode 0600, with [daemon] launch = "systemd", a file already there refused, never edited; checks as the account that karvi config show daemon.launch says systemd, so that a global file setting config.allow-user-layer = false is found; checks that the package's template unit is installed, refusing without it, and runs systemctl enable --now karvi-daemon@karvi.service; checks karvi daemon status as the account; each part entered in the record /etc/karvi/service-karvi.installed as it is made or found (below). The record states that the unit runs the daemon as the account with the configuration karvi reads for it, the global file (/etc/karvi/config.toml, else /opt/karvi/config.toml, the first that exists) and then the account's own, named by its full path, and lists what the install made as against what it found. daemon remove undoes what the record lists, in reverse: systemctl disable --now of the instance, the stop waiting for its jobs under the daemon's grace as at a shutdown; and the configuration file and the group membership, each when the install made it. The account and its home stay, and the record keeps their lines; under --purge the account's files in the shared trees and the shared scratch go to root, and the account with its home, when the install made it, and the record go too (below). What the install found is left, and so are the template unit, the package's, and the shared trees, which hold every operator's work. karvi reads no configuration file in a private root: only the global file, the account's ~/.config/karvi/config.toml, and --config. Not taken: the home /var/lib/karvi (above); karvi-service (at the operator's word, a name for root's system tasks); the bare install and remove (read as installing karvi); the script in /usr/share/karvi (not on root's path) or scripts/ (the tree's test and release tools, not shipped); karvi setup service in Go (the operator's bash, its work useradd and systemctl).

Issue 16, continued: the template unit's place, agreed. What it gains: the unit an instance runs is the installed release's, where a copy the install made into /etc/systemd/system from /usr/share/karvi/systemd/system would keep its settings through every later upgrade without a word, this chapter's own KillMode and TimeoutStopSec among them. It waits on nothing. The rule. The package installs the template where systemd finds a package's units, /usr/lib/systemd/system/karvi-daemon@.service, the one unit it installs there, and an upgrade replaces it. A template runs nothing until an instance is enabled, so nothing the package installs is active until the site chooses, as before. The package never enables, starts, or restarts an instance (issue 7): dh_installsystemd makes no maintainer-script snippet for a unit named with @ (/usr/bin/dh_installsystemd, read, not run), so the rules need no override. A site's own settings go in a drop-in, /etc/systemd/system/karvi-daemon@.service.d/, which an upgrade never touches. karvi-sysutil copies no unit: daemon install refuses without the template (karvi-daemon@.service not installed; install the karvi package), and daemon remove leaves it. An install from the release bundle places the file as BUILD-HOWTO section 10 says. Not taken: the install's copy into /etc/systemd/system (stale after every upgrade); systemctl link (a second way of placing a unit for the administrator to recognise); daemon install run again after each upgrade to refresh the copy (a step to forget).

Issue 16, continued: the reload at an upgrade, agreed. What it gains: the administrator's restart after an upgrade runs the new release's unit. It waits on the template's place (above). Found: an upgrade replaces the template's file and systemd keeps the unit it loaded. On a runtime user template standing for it, its file replaced while an instance ran: a restart without a daemon-reload warned that the file had changed on disk and ran the old unit, its KillMode and its command; a daemon-reload alone gave the running instance the new KillMode at once, its pid the same, and the new command at its next restart. dh_installsystemd makes no reload for a template, and systemd's dpkg triggers watch no unit directory. The rule. The package runs systemctl --system daemon-reload itself, as debhelper's snippets do for any other unit: packaging/debian/karvi.postinst at configure and dpkg's abort- cases, packaging/debian/karvi.postrm at remove, each when systemd runs (/run/systemd/system exists) and DPKG_ROOT is empty, a failure ignored. It enables, starts, and restarts nothing. After an upgrade the administrator's one step is systemctl restart karvi-daemon@karvi.service. Not taken: the administrator's own daemon-reload before the restart (forgotten, the restart runs the old unit with a warning alone).

Issue 16, continued: what a removal keeps, and --purge, agreed. What it gains: no later account takes over the service account's files. It waits on nothing. Found: with the shared trees in place, the account's home holds its configuration, its trust store, and the daemon's log and state; its jobs, collection files, and transcripts are in the shared trees, and its scoreboards, the ledger files it last wrote, and its scratch in the shared scratch, all owned by its uid (FILES section 2). adduser --system gives a new account the lowest free uid from 100 (first_avail_uid in /usr/sbin/adduser, read, not run): an account removed hands its uid to the next system account a package makes, which would own the service account's jobs and collections, devices' configurations among them, and could open them to anyone. The rule. daemon remove stops and disables the instance and removes the configuration file and the group membership, each when the install made it; the account and its home stay, its files keeping their owner, and a later daemon install takes the account back with its trust store; the record keeps its lines for the account and its home, so that a later daemon remove --purge knows the install made them. daemon remove --purge does the same, then gives every file the account owns in the shared trees and the shared scratch to root, its group and mode unchanged, so that the operators read them still and no later account owns them; removes the account and its home, when the install made it; and removes the record. Not taken: the account removed by a plain daemon remove (its uid reused); its files left in the shared trees under a removed uid at --purge (the same); its files there removed at --purge (other operators' jobs sit in day folders it made, and they are the site's records).

Issue 16, continued: an install or a removal run again, agreed. What it gains: an install that failed partway is finished by running it again, or undone, where a record written last would leave none: its account taken as found by the next run, and so never removed, and its configuration file refused. It waits on nothing. The rule. The install enters each part in the record as it makes or finds it, so that a failed install leaves the list of what it did. daemon install reads the record: each part it lists is checked and reported exists, a part missing is made, and the two checks, daemon.launch and daemon status, always run; run again on a whole install, it changes nothing and reports each part exists, as karvi setup shared does, and after a plain daemon remove it takes the account back and makes the rest. A configuration file the record does not list is refused, as before. A --group other than the one whose membership the record lists is refused, the two stacked, naming daemon remove. daemon remove reports a part already gone absent, and without a record is refused: no service installed: /etc/karvi/service-karvi.installed absent. Not taken: a second install refused outright (a failed one cleaned by hand); the record written last (above).

Issue 16, continued: no dry run, and an install that repairs, agreed. What it gains: a refused install leaves the host as it was, and an install run over an existing one sets right what has drifted from what it made. It waits on nothing. The rule. karvi-sysutil has no --dry-run: daemon install checks every refusal before it changes anything (root, the template installed, the group, an account karvi that is not a system user, a configuration file the record does not list, a --group other than the record's, the recorded uid held by another account), so that a refusal changes nothing and a failure partway is an error it did not foresee, which the record covers; the manual page lists the steps. Over an existing install, daemon install repairs each part the record lists as made: a part missing is made again, the account with the uid the record holds, so that its files keep their owner; the account's home and login shell, the home's owner and mode, the configuration file's owner and mode (the account's, 0600), and the group membership are set back; and the instance is enabled and started when it is not, after systemctl reset-failed when it failed. Each part is reported made, exists, or repaired, a repaired part's value as found over the value set, stacked. It repairs neither the configuration file's content, which the administrator may have added to (a daemon.launch other than systemd is refused, stacked, naming the file), nor a running daemon of another build, which waits on the administrator's restart (issue 7), the status naming it. Not taken: --dry-run (a second path through the script to keep in step with the first, its answer only as good as what it can check before anything is made); a repair that rewrites the configuration file (the administrator's additions lost); a repair that restarts the daemon (the restart's moment the administrator's).

Issue 16, continued: the test, in a container, agreed. What it gains: karvi-sysutil, the package's template and maintainer scripts, and the account's daemon tested as root on an Ubuntu 26.04 host that is not this one, at the operator's word, so that nothing here needs sudo or changes. It waits on the S5 build. Found: ubuntu:26.04 (Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, systemd 259.5) with systemd its PID 1 under Docker 29.8.2, without --privileged; as Docker runs it, systemd exits 255, Failed to create /init.scope control group: Read-only file system, and with --cap-add SYS_ADMIN alone the same; with SYS_ADMIN, AppArmor unconfined, a private cgroup namespace, and an entrypoint that remounts /sys/fs/cgroup writable, it runs with no unit failed, logind and sshd up. In it, logind removed an ordinary user's /dev/shm file 13 s after the user's ssh session ended and kept a system user's, and docker stop, systemd's halt signal, waited out a unit's 8-s stop, systemd exiting 0, as on this host (issue 14). jobs/261016/261016-091500-00

Every folder holds summary.json (2,603 bytes for the run of two devices), which names the job, its start and end, its status, its exit, and its device counts. The run with the unreachable device is errored, ExitPartialFailure 101, one of two devices failed, its folder holding failed-devices.txt with the device's name; the others are completed, ExitSuccess 0. A command writes a folder as a run does, and two jobs in one second take -00 and -01. The Kiritimati run started at 15:15:00 EDT by its summary's started_at, and its ID and day folder name that zone's date, 261016, while the host's was the 15th; the run 33 seconds later, 261015-151533-00, sorts before it. The manifest, which names the operator and the selection, was 19,288 bytes for the two devices.

What it gains. An operator finds a job's ID, its result, and its folder without listing day folders and reading JSON: the ID job follow and job cancel take, and the failed-devices.txt a rerun takes (--tf).

What it waits on. Nothing: every finished job writes its summary, and the list needs no daemon or credential; issue 2 moves the job summary schema from 3 to 4.

Its issues, one at a time: what it lists with no option; the filters; the columns at a terminal's width and the rows' order; another operator's jobs in shared mode; and a run under --nof, which leaves no folder.

Issue 1, what it lists with no option, agreed. On the lab above. The rule. With no option, job list lists the newest 20 jobs of the operator's output root, whatever their day: it reads the day folders newest first and stops once it has 20, a running or unfinished job counting among them. Twenty lines and a header fit a terminal of 24. Why: it always answers, whatever the day or the timezone, and its cost does not grow with the retention. Not taken: today's folder (empty after midnight, or holding only the 02:15 collection of packaging/cron/karvi-crun; and which folder is today follows the effective timezone, as the Kiritimati run's did); the last 24 hours (empty on a quiet day, and every summary in the window read for its start); every job kept (31 days at karvi-prune's default, the daily collection alone 31 lines).

Issue 2, the filters, agreed. On the lab above and two measurements. A copy of the errored run's summary in 1,240 job folders, 31 days of 40, was read and decoded whole in 38 and 61 ms (Python, the page cache warm), so a filter can read back through every day kept. The summary names no device, its device_counts the counts alone. commands.jsonl names one in every record (device.canonical_name, beside operator, activity_type, and command) and carries the output: a run of the fake's 65.7 MB show big wrote a commands.jsonl of 66,605,035 bytes, read once for a name in 161 and 177 ms, beside a summary of 2,549 bytes. The manifest names the devices the selection resolved to (plan.targets, beside the inputs as typed in selection), 19,288 bytes for two devices. Where output.<device>.txt is kept, its name answers:

$ ls jobs/*/*/output.dead-iosxe.txt
jobs/261015/261015-151449-01/output.dead-iosxe.txt

A site may turn off every output file but the summary and commands.jsonl, and there the operator's question, what was run at a device and by whom, needs the list by device. The rule. job list takes three filters, each judging the job and applied before the count. --last N is the count, 20 by default, 0 every job kept, as karvi-prune's --minfree 0 turns its floor off. --failed keeps the finished jobs whose exit is not 0, a partial failure and a cancellation among them; an unfinished job has no exit and is left out. --target NAME keeps the jobs that reached a device, NAME taken as run's --target takes it (lowercased, a glob, repeatable, a job matching when any of its devices does); the named device's own outcome is issue 3's. The job summary names the job's devices, each with its outcome (one of device_counts' five), so the search reads summaries alone: job summary schema 3 to 4. An unfinished job, without a summary, is matched from the records its commands.jsonl holds so far. Why: the searches an operator makes, at the cost of the file every site keeps, which holds across the retention. Not taken: --all (in run and crun every device of the inventory, and a second option for one limit); each job's commands.jsonl searched (the cost grows with the output kept, not with the devices); the manifest (its size grows with the plan, and it is a switch a site turns off); the name of output.<device>.txt (a switch too); --failed judged by a named device's outcome (one option with two meanings); dates, --day or --since (the effective timezone's question again, answered by --last 0); the kind of job, a column; the operator, issue 4. Found: the audit's command_completed names its device inside KARVI_AUDIT_JSON alone, which journalctl matches only whole, and a run under --nof leaves no folder while its event still names the device; a KARVI_DEVICE field is ROADMAP Later, on the operator's word.

Issue 2, continued: the summary written at acceptance, agreed. A run of show slow at 20 seconds, killed (kill -9) after 3, left 261015-160057-00 with a manifest of 17,368 bytes, a commands.txt of 10, and a commands.jsonl and an errors.jsonl of 0, though the fake had been sent the command; its manifest's plan.targets named fake-iosxe, its records nothing. A job's summary is written last, and InspectJobDirectory, which job follow reads, takes its presence for the job's end; karvi-prune reads its final_status and keeps a folder whose summary is not final as live. The operator's word: the devices go in the summary, since many sites turn the manifest off. The rule. A job's summary.json is written when the job is accepted, naming its devices with no outcome and none of the result fields, and written whole again at its end; a job is finished when its summary names a final status. InspectJobDirectory and job follow's path through the folder read the status, not the file's presence; the pruner takes a summary that is not final as it takes a folder without one, under the age rule alone; FILES section 4.3's "written last" becomes written at the job's acceptance and again at its end. An unfinished job is then matched by --target from its summary like any other. Why: a job cut short at any point names its devices in the one file every site keeps. Not taken: the manifest's plan.targets first where it is kept, proposed first (a site that turns it off loses the job); the records alone, issue 2's first rule (a job killed before its first record matches nothing); a file of the devices beside the summary (a switch a site turns off too).

Issue 3, the columns and the rows' order, agreed with the operator's two additions. On the lab above. watch --format table, under a pseudo-terminal of 80 columns, printed its header in 89 cells and its rows in 93 to 104, 83 of them before TARGET: a table it never narrows. Its TIME is a finished job's end, HH:MM:SS, without the date; its MODE says run or cmd; it orders the finished jobs newest first by their end, the Kiritimati run among them in its place by time. The site's display.timestamp (hh:mm:ss yyyy-mm-dd) takes 19 cells. A sketch, laid out by a script from the lab's summaries and not printed by karvi, with OPERATOR shown, left TARGET 7 cells at 80 columns, +12 for a job of twelve devices (wide-001 to wide-012); at 120, five names and +7; at 160, nine and +3; to a pipe, all twelve in a line of 180. The rule. The text is watch's table, its headings, cells, and status colours from the code watch uses (Duration, DoneCell, the heading line), but: no ACTV, a folder holding no live count; TIME the job's duration, its start being its ID; MODE the kind of job, cmd, run, or crun (an exercise is run, its STATUS exercised), four cells; and OPERATOR always, on the operator's word. The line fits the terminal's width, read at each run as watch reads it, with no limit at 80: TARGET takes what the fixed columns leave, each name whole while it fits and the rest counted, +N; to a pipe or a file nothing is cut. The rows stand in job-ID order, newest first, an unfinished job in its place with STATUS unfinished and TIME blank. Under --target, on the operator's word, a row is one matching device: JOB-ID, TIME, OPERATOR, MODE, OUTCOME (the device's own), and DEVICE, 59 cells before DEVICE, and --last counts rows. --format json prints one array of the rows, each the job's summary fields and its folder's path, under --target also the device and its outcome. Why: watch's words and code, a line that fits its terminal, and no read beyond issues 1 and 2's. Not taken: watch's table as it is (it wraps at 80); the end with its date (19 cells); the order of the start instants (every summary read for an order the ID gives but across a changed timezone, where the Kiritimati run stands first by its ID and no cell contradicts it, its TIME a duration); watch's running rows above a rule (a folder's unfinished job may be days dead); a name cut (fake-iosxe de in the first sketch); a limit at 80 columns; under --target, the device's outcome in TARGET (dead-iosxe=failed, 17 cells, +1 at 80). Found: watch --all-retained is registered as not built, from before the public tree, with no specification; job list --last 0 is that view, and the placeholder goes when job list is built.

Issue 4, another operator's jobs in shared mode, agreed. A lab of two operators, netops and netops.test, both of the group netops, each with its own configuration, base directory, and trust store and one shared root in /dev/shm (group netops, its jobs tree 2770), each running one job:

$ ls -ld shared/jobs/*/*
drwxr-s--- 2 netops      netops 200 Oct 15 17:01 261015/261015-170121-00
drwxr-s--- 2 netops.test netops 200 Oct 15 17:01 261015/261015-170122-00

Both jobs stand in the one tree, every file 0640 in the operators' group; netops read netops.test's summary, whose manifest names operator: netops.test. The daemon refuses a client whose UID is not its own, so a job's files are its operator's, a service account's job the service account's. job follow by netops of netops.test's finished job exited 111, run_output_records_unreadable: …/commands.jsonl is owned by uid 1001, not 1000: the folder's path opens commands.jsonl only when it is the caller's own, while FILES section 4.3 says any member reads another's job with karvi job follow ID. The rule. job list reads the output root issue 1 names: in shared mode every job of the shared tree, every operator's and a service account's; in individual mode the operator's own. OPERATOR is the owner of the job's summary, named by the system's user database, the UID where it names none. --operator NAME, repeatable, keeps that operator's jobs, applied before the count as the other filters are. A folder the operator cannot read is listed with ? in the flag column, as watch marks an unreadable file. job follow, in the shared tree, takes a file another member owns when its group is the tree's and its mode 0640 or stricter, its other checks (a regular file, no link followed) as they are, so FILES holds. Why: the question that brought --target, whether any operator, agent, or application ran a job at a device, is answered by the shared tree, and the owner is the file system's word, not a file's. Not taken: the operator's own jobs by default, another's on an option (the question is everyone's); OPERATOR from a field of the summary (the same value, which a crafted file could name otherwise); FILES changed to the folder's path (a listed job that cannot be followed); an unreadable folder left out (a list that hides what is there).

Issue 4, continued: another member's live job followed from its folder, agreed. On the lab of two operators, with both configurations' scoreboards in one shared directory (3770, group netops) as a site's scratch root has them, netops started a run of show slow at 25 seconds through its daemon (--detach, 261015-170932-00). While it ran, netops.test's watch --format table showed it, running, netops, 0/1, one device in flight; its job follow exited 112, job_orphaned: job 261015-170932-00: … holds no summary and no running daemon holds the job … the daemon that ran it is gone, though the job was live; netops's own follow rendered it to its end, exit 0, elapsed=25.62s. A follow asks the caller's own daemon, which holds its own jobs alone and refuses another UID, and then the folder, which it reads for a finished job only. The rule. job follow of a job no daemon of the caller's holds, whose summary is not final, follows its folder: it renders each record of commands.jsonl as it is written and ends when the summary names a final status, the follow's display ending as it does for a job that has ended. It answers job_orphaned only when the job's scoreboard is stale by watch's rule (watch.stale-after) or is gone. A site that turns commands.jsonl off sees such a job at its end alone. Why: job list shows another member's running jobs, and following one is the next thing an operator does; issue 2's summary at acceptance says the job is running, and issue 4's rule lets a member read its files. Not taken: a daemon serving followers of another UID (the daemon's one boundary crossed); the false job_orphaned recorded as a defect and the follow across members left for later.

Issue 5, a job without a folder and the summary's switch, agreed. On the lab: a run under --nof left no folder (seven before and after) while its command_completed audit event named fake-iosxe and the job, and output.persist-command = false does the same for every job on every path. A run with output.files.summary-json=false completed, exit 0, and left a folder without a summary; job follow 261015-171544-00 answered job_orphaned, exit 112. The operator's rule. Every job that makes a folder writes its summary: output.files.summary-json is removed, and the summary is the folder's index, which the list, the follow, the live follow, and the pruner read. An operator or a site may choose no output, --nof or output.persist-command = false, and the job then makes no folder, no summary, and no other file, and job list does not list it, with no warning. A folder without a summary is then a job cut short before its summary's first write: unfinished, and orphaned by the stale scoreboard's rule alone. The configuration registry loses the key and moves; the generated reference, schema, and ERROR-CODES follow it; job_orphaned loses its clause on the switch; FILES section 4.3 names the summary as always written. Why: the list's one source is wherever a folder is, and no output stays the operator's choice. Not taken: the switch kept and the functions it costs documented (a row that cannot say what the job did, a follow without its end, no follow across members), proposed and set aside on the operator's word; --nof writing the summary alone (the choice of nothing on disk overridden). Beyond the list, on the operator's word: what karvi writes to journald, and so to the syslog a host forwards it to, does not suffice as the audit trail, a later improvement (ROADMAP Later); after it, an audit review tool, perhaps the administrators', can answer for every job, while job list answers an operator for the jobs they made and, on a shared host, the team's.

Issue 4, continued while building: a job without a scoreboard, agreed. On a lab of the two operators, one shared tree and one scoreboard folder, with the follow from the folder built: netops ran show slow under --set watch.enabled=false (--detach, 261015-215025-00), no scoreboard was written for it, and netops.test's job follow answered at once, exit 112, job_orphaned: job 261015-215025-00 has no final summary and no scoreboard. A run killed with SIGKILL 2 seconds in (261015-215338-01) was followed by netops.test until its scoreboard went stale, 8 seconds later, exit 112, the refusal stacking the scoreboard's last update over watch.stale-after. The rule, as issue 4's continuation had it. With no scoreboard nothing shows the job running, and the follow from its folder answers job_orphaned at once, its words naming the fact; a site that turns watch.enabled off cannot follow another member's live job, while each operator follows their own through their daemon. Why: the scoreboard is the one sign of a live job that a member can read. Not taken: following on without a scoreboard (a dead job's follow never ends, and every long-dead job has none, scoreboards being pruned); the summary naming whether the job keeps a scoreboard (a field, and a dead job's follow on such a site still never ends).

Issue 4, continued while building: a job without commands.jsonl, agreed. On the same lab, a run of show slow under --set output.files.commands-jsonl=false (261015-222039-00) left a folder without commands.jsonl, its summary's paths naming none, as the summary is built "so no reader is sent to a file that will not exist". netops's follow through its daemon rendered the job live, exit 0, and after its end showed the footer and warning: records 1 to 1 were before this follow and are not kept (output.files.commands-jsonl is false); netops.test's follow from the folder, and netops's once its daemon was stopped, exited 111, run_output_records_unreadable: open …/commands.jsonl: no such file or directory, as a finished job's follow from its folder did before. The rule. When the job's summary names no commands_jsonl in its paths, the follow from its folder opens no file and renders no record: it writes one warning, the job's records are not kept (output.files.commands-jsonl is false), waits until the summary is final under the rule above, and ends with the display's end from summary.json (the footer, the summary line under --format jsonl, [] under json) and the job's exit, at once for a finished job. Whether the summary names the file counts, never the path it names; a summary naming commands_jsonl whose file is missing stays run_output_records_unreadable. A job that keeps commands.jsonl is rendered record by record as it is written. Built, netops.test's follow of such a job (261015-225241-00) printed the warning and the footer, exit 0, as netops's from the folder did after its end. Why: the follow from the folder ends as the daemon's follow of the same job ends. Not taken: no warning, the setting being deliberate (the follower may not be the one who chose it, and the daemon's follow warns); the file's absence alone (a lost file and one never written alike).

Issue 4, continued while building: a job ended without its final summary, agreed. On the same lab, a run of show slow (--detach, 261015-225412-00) whose folder the lab's script made unwritable 2 seconds in ended as a full output disk would end it: netops's follow through its daemon showed ! exit=111, the scoreboard and watch said errored, and the summary was still the one written at acceptance. A job writes its final scoreboard before its final summary, and a scoreboard naming a final status is never stale by watch's rule, so netops.test's follow from the folder rendered the record and waited until the script stopped it after 60 seconds, saying the job continued. The rule. While the summary is not final, a scoreboard that names the job's end is stale once its last update is older than watch.stale-after, as any other is; the follow then answers job_orphaned, its words saying the scoreboard ended and stacking its last update over watch.stale-after. watch keeps its own rule. Built, the same run (261015-230251-00) was followed by netops.test to job_orphaned: job 261015-230251-00 has no final summary and its scoreboard ended errored, exit 112, 29 seconds after the job's start. Why: the follow ends with a true answer where the job's own end left no summary. Not taken: ending as soon as the scoreboard names an end (the summary's last write follows the scoreboard's, and one read could fall between them); ending with the scoreboard's status as the result (it holds no exit); a new code (job_orphaned already names a job without a final summary).

Issue 3, continued while building: the kind of job in the summary, agreed. On a lab of the S2 tree (47105b9), one operator: a command, a run, a crun, a run --exercise, and a crun --exercise, each finished, and a detached run and crun of show slow read 2 seconds after their acceptance. Every summary's mode was live, or exercise for the two exercises, the plan's mode; nothing in it told a command from a run, and collection was present for the finished crun alone, absent from both exercises and from the live crun's summary, written at acceptance. Their scoreboards' mode said cmd, run, crun, exercise, and exercise. A job of stream, with or without --cd=PATH, and a run --cd=PATH were run by their scoreboards, the last two with collection present: a collection is not a crun. The rule. The summary names the job's kind, kind, at its acceptance and at its end: cmd for a command, crun for a crun, and run for a run and a job of stream; job list's MODE shows it. An exercise keeps its kind, its STATUS exercised, so an exercised crun is crun. mode stays live or exercise. Job summary schema 4, not yet released, takes the field. Why: MODE from the one file the list reads, for every job, an unfinished one among them. Not taken: activity_type (command or run, as the records name it; a crun is not told at its acceptance); the scoreboard's words in the summary's mode (an existing field's meaning changed, an exercise's kind lost); the scoreboard or the manifest (pruned sooner, or a switch a site turns off); collection (absent at acceptance, and present for a run --cd).

Issue 2, continued while building: a --target beginning with !, agreed. On the same lab: run --dry-run --target '*-iosxe' --target '!dead*' planned one target, and run --dry-run --target '!dead*' exited 5, inventory_positive_selector_missing: … a value beginning with "!" only removes devices. A run of fake-iosxe and dead-iosxe (261016-002853-00, exit 101) left a summary naming fake-iosxe succeeded and dead-iosxe failed. The rule. job list's --target values are applied to each job's devices, its summary's devices, as run applies them to the inventory: a value that selects keeps the devices it matches, and one beginning with ! removes the devices it matches, wherever it stands. A job is listed when one of its devices remains, and under --target each remaining device is a row. A line whose every --target value begins with ! is refused before any folder is read, as run refuses it, inventory_positive_selector_missing, exit 5, its words naming job list. On that job, --target '*-iosxe' --target '!dead*' gives one row, fake-iosxe succeeded; --target 'dead*' one row, dead-iosxe failed; --target '!dead*' alone the refusal. Why: --target means in job list what it means in run, the removal among it, and no line lists nothing without saying why. Not taken: ! refused in job list (the option no longer run's); ! alone meaning every device but those (run's rule broken, one option with two meanings); ! alone listing nothing (an empty list without its reason).

Issue 4, continued while building: an unreadable folder's row, agreed. On the same lab, three finished jobs made unreadable by the lab's script: 261016-003305-00's summary given mode 000, 261016-003307-00's cut to 100 bytes, and 261016-003309-00's folder given mode 000. Each one's job follow exited 111, the first and the third run_output_records_unreadable: … permission denied, the second run_output_record_decode_failed: … unexpected end of JSON input. The summary's owner was found for the first two, netops, and for the third only the folder's; watch --format table, with a scoreboard file of mode 000, showed it ? 261016-003305-00 - invalid - - - - - and the file's path in TARGET. The rule. A job folder whose summary cannot be read or decoded is a ? row; a folder without one is unfinished. Its cells are watch's invalid row's: ? in the flag column, JOB-ID the folder's name, STATUS invalid, - in TIME, MODE, DONE, and FAIL, TARGET the summary's path; OPERATOR is the summary's owner, or the folder's where the summary cannot be reached, which the file system names when the file cannot be read. --operator judges the row by that owner; --failed and --target cannot judge it and keep it, and --last counts it. Under --target the row's OUTCOME is invalid and its DEVICE the path. --format json gives it as {"path", "operator", "error"}, as watch's JSON gives {"path", "error"}. The exit stays 0, with no warning, as watch's. Why: the list shows every folder under every filter, and --operator still judges each. Not taken: the row left out under --failed or --target (a job that may match hidden); OPERATOR - (the owner is known, and --operator could not judge the row); a warning or another exit (the list answered).

Issue 3, continued while building: an unfinished job's counts, agreed with the operator's refinement. On the same lab, a detached run of fake-iosxe and dead-iosxe (261016-003707-00) while it ran, and a run under --no-daemon killed with SIGKILL 2 seconds in (261016-003708-00): each summary, the one written at acceptance, named its devices without an outcome and held no final_status and no device_counts. watch --format table --stale-after 4s showed the first running, DONE 0/2, FAIL 0, ACTV 1, and the second the same with !, the killed job's last counts. The rule. An unfinished job's DONE shows u, unknown, over the number of its summary's devices, the slash under DONE's O as in every row (u/2), and its FAIL shows u; the two u and STATUS unfinished take the warning colour, never written into a file. TIME stays blank, and TARGET names the devices as for any job. Under --target the row's OUTCOME is unfinished, in the warning colour, and its TIME blank. --format json gives the summary's fields as written at acceptance, with path and operator, and under --target device without outcome, the summary's device having none. A sketch, laid out by a script and not printed by karvi:

  JOB-ID            TIME      STATUS      OPERATOR  MODE    DONE   FAIL  TARGET
  261016-003708-00            unfinished  netops    run     u/1       u  fake-iosxe
  261016-003707-00            unfinished  netops    run     u/2       u  fake-iosxe dead-iosxe
  261016-002853-00  0m04s     errored     netops    run     2/2       1  fake-iosxe dead-iosxe

Why: every cell from the summary alone, and none naming a count not known; u, not ?, which reads as a digit's place and is the flag column's mark of an unreadable folder; the warning colour, since the job may run or be dead, and the error colour is FAIL's for failed devices. Not taken: the scoreboard's live counts (a second read for some rows, gone under watch.enabled = false or once pruned, and a dead job's last counts not its end); 0/2 and 0 (counts not known shown as none done and none failed); a blank FAIL, proposed first; - (watch's mark of a file not read); the error colour.

Issue 3, continued while building: OPERATOR in the JSON, agreed. On the same lab, the finished job 261016-003707-00: its scoreboard and its manifest named operator as {"username":"netops","uid":1000,"primary_gid":1000, "groups":[…]}, its summary named none, and stat named the summary's owner netops, UID 1000. The summary names no operator by issue 4's rule, so the rows issue 3 gave as the summary's fields and the folder's path held no OPERATOR. The rule. Each row of job list --format json is one object: the summary's fields as the file holds them, then path, the job's folder, and operator, {"username", "uid"}, the shape the scoreboard and the manifest use, from the summary's owner as the list finds it, the folder's for a ? row; username is "" where the user database names none, and the table then shows the UID. Under --target the row adds device and outcome, outcome left out for an unfinished job; a ? row is {"path", "operator", "error"}. summary.json is unchanged. Why: a script reads what the table shows, and --operator's judgement can be checked on every row. Not taken: operator as the cell's text (a name not told from a UID); the whole operator with its groups (a second lookup for values nothing reads); no operator (the one column the summary cannot give missing). Found: watch shows the scoreboard's operator.username, which the job's process writes, and never reads the file's owner, so a scoreboard in the shared folder (3770) naming another operator is shown under that name, where job list names the owner; watch's OPERATOR from the owner is ROADMAP Later, on the operator's word.

Issue 1, continued while building: an empty list, agreed. On a lab of the working tree, job list --operator nobody exited 0 and printed (no jobs). The rule. A list with no rows prints the one line (no jobs) on stdout, exit 0, as watch --format table prints (no retained activities): for an empty output root, one not yet made, and filters that leave nothing alike. job list makes no folder, taking the base folder's path as watch takes it. --format json prints []. Why: a list without rows says so. Not taken: the heading alone (a list that reads as cut short); nothing (an empty answer not told from a failure); a warning on stderr (an empty list is no fault).

Issue 4, continued while building: an unreadable folder's row at a terminal, agreed. On the same lab, under script(1) at 80 columns, job list --last 4 printed its heading in 79 cells and its rows in 75, and each ? row in 144, its TARGET the summary's path, 72 cells where 7 were left; a site's path, /opt/karvi/shared/jobs/261016/261016-010107-00/summary.json, is 59 cells and fits whole from 132 columns. The rule. At a terminal a ? row's TARGET, or its DEVICE under --target, is the summary's path when it fits whole and … when it does not, the mark of text left out as watch's cut uses it; to a pipe or a file the path is whole. The row still names the job, its owner, and invalid, and --format json (path, error) or job follow ID, whose refusal names both, gives the path and the reason. Why: every row fits the terminal, as the table's rule has it. Not taken: the path whole, as built first (the one row that wraps); the path cut at its start or its end (7 cells at 80 say nothing, and a name cut is issue 3's not taken); - (watch's mark of no value, where one was left out); the error's words (as wide at 80, and new words in a cell).

Issue 4, continued while building: a day folder that cannot be read, agreed. On a lab of the working tree, two runs on the 16th and one under --timezone Pacific/Honolulu, whose day folder was the 15th's, and then 261016 given mode 000 by the lab's script: job list exited 0 and listed ? 261016 - invalid netops, the folder's path in TARGET, and then the Honolulu run, 261015-193306-00, completed; --format json gave the folder's row as its path, its owner, and run_output_records_unreadable: read …/jobs/261016: open …: permission denied. The rule. A day folder the operator cannot read is one ? row in its day's place: JOB-ID the folder's name, STATUS invalid, - in the other cells, OPERATOR the folder's owner, TARGET (DEVICE under --target) the folder's path or … at a terminal where it does not fit. The filters take it as a ? job folder: --operator judges it, --failed and --target keep it, and --last counts it as one row. --format json gives {"path", "operator", "error"}, and the exit is 0. Why: the list goes on past the folder and shows it is there. Not taken: the list refused, exit 111 (every other day hidden by one folder); a warning and the day passed over (the table silent where it is, the JSON without it); a row per job (their IDs cannot be read).

Issue 4, continued while building: a job whose day folder cannot be read, followed, agreed. On a lab of 47105b9, job follow of a job whose folder the lab's script gave mode 000 exited 111, run_output_records_unreadable: read …/summary.json: … permission denied, and of a job whose day folder it gave mode 000 exited 112, job_unknown: no job 261016-015352-00: … does not exist: LocateJobDirectory took every lstat failure for an absent folder. The rule. job follow takes a job folder that lstat cannot reach, for any reason but its absence, as found, and its check names why, run_output_records_unreadable, exit 111, as for a job folder it cannot read; the daemon is asked first, as before. Built, the same follow exited 111, run_output_records_unreadable: …/261016/261016-015356-00: lstat …: permission denied. Why: the follow's answer is true, and the operator looks at the folder's mode or group. Not taken: the answer left (a false one); a new code (the one that names an unreadable folder, at the same exit as a job folder's); the other day folders searched first (the derived folder is where the job was written, and a glob sees no more through an unreadable folder).

Issue 5, continued while building: a folder without a summary, agreed. On a lab of the working tree, a run through the daemon without NETPASS exited 6, credential_prompt_unavailable: client planning: …, and left 261016-020953-00 empty, the folder the daemon had made for it (ROADMAP Later); job list showed it unfinished, MODE blank, DONE u/0, FAIL u, TARGET blank. A job writes its summary at its acceptance before any device is contacted, so a folder without one reached no device. The rule. A job folder without a summary is unfinished, STATUS unfinished and TIME blank; MODE u, DONE u/u, and FAIL u, every u in the warning colour, its kind and its count of devices not known; TARGET blank, no device reached. --target leaves it out, as a job that reached no device, --failed as an unfinished job, and --operator judges it by the folder's owner. --format json gives {"path", "operator"}, there being no summary's fields. Why: the row claims nothing not known, and --target answers truly for it. Not taken: u/0 and a blank MODE, as built first (a count of none claimed, a blank read as a missing column); a ? row (nothing failed to be read: the folder holds no summary); the row kept under --target, as a ? row is (a ? row may hide a match, and this folder cannot).

The code moved the bytes: karvi is 69,632 bytes larger, karvi-prune 4,096, karvi-askpass the same size with other bytes; the bundle is 76,779 bytes larger and the package 31,272. go-version-m.txt is 0.30.1's; the default configuration has no output.files.summary-json. Issue 1, the native suite's S33 check, agreed. The artifacts' first run stopped in the bundle's own verifier at S33 hook timeout: the hook's child outlived it. The check (scripts/native-smoke-test.sh, line 870) runs pgrep -f "sleep 20" across the whole host just after crun returns from a crun.after hook it ended at a one-second bound, and on a match pkill -f 'sleep 20'. The same check had passed in both release verifier runs; alone from the same extraction S33 passed five times in five, and the bound's signalling in a plain shell left the hook's sleep behind in none of 300 runs on the host as it was. Whether the hook's sleep was not yet gone under the verifier's three lanes, or another process matched, is not settled: other work's containers were being started and stopped on the host at the time. The second run passed whole, the same bundle bytes. What it gains: S33 fails only for the suite's own processes and ends no other: any sleep 20… on the host, another project's, another operator's, or another lane's, failed it, and its pkill then ended that process and every shell whose command line held the pattern. What it waits on: nothing. The rule, the operator's: a suite looks for, and ends, only processes it started: by a PID or process group it recorded, or by a pattern holding its own work directory; never by a pattern another process on the host can match. Line 870 is the only breach: line 757 names $TMP, and the v0100 suite's serving() keeps the daemons whose command line holds its base directory. The check: the hook writes $$, the process group it leads, and after crun returns pgrep -g that group, given two seconds to empty, and on failure kill -KILL -PGID that group alone (dash, which runs the suite, refuses kill -KILL -- -PGID). In a copy of the bundle's extraction, beside an unrelated sleep 200 (the bystander), the check as released and the check drafted ([script] lines are the lab script's; [suite] lines the suite's exit and its last line):

the check as released:

the check drafted, the copy's hook child ignoring SIGTERM:
[suite] run 1 exit=1: native smoke: FAIL: S33 hook timeout: the hook's group 3235694 outlived it
[script] bystander pid 3234497 still running

Not taken: a narrower pkill pattern, which can still match another's process; a sleep copied under $TMP so that the pattern holds the work directory, more machinery for the same scope. The control above found karvi's own bound short of what its documents say, issue 2; with issue 2 in, the check has no wait, looking at the group when crun returns, and the suite's hook child ignores SIGTERM, so that the suite proves the kill.

Issue 2, the crun.after bound, agreed. collectionHook.run (internal/app/crun_after.go) sent SIGTERM to the hook's process group at the bound, and os/exec's kill five seconds on (WaitDelay) reached the hook's shell alone, and only when the shell was still there: a child ignoring SIGTERM outlived crun, where COLLECTION, crun.after-timeout's documentation, and the code's comment said the group was killed. What it gains: a hook past its bound, or interrupted, leaves nothing running, as the documents say, and issue 1's check needs no wait. What it waits on: nothing. The rule, the operator's: when karvi signals a hook's process group, at its bound or at the invocation's interrupt, it returns only once the group is gone: SIGTERM to the group; SIGKILL to whatever is left of it five seconds later; then up to five seconds more for the killed processes to go, a process that will not die even then (in uninterruptible sleep) left. A hook that exits on its own is not followed: whatever it leaves in its group is its own. The duration the warning and the audit report is the hook's own, up to the end of its shell. The change: the Cancel function notes when it signalled; after Run, endGroup looks at the group every 20 ms (kill(-pgid, 0) until ESRCH), sends SIGKILL at the signal plus five seconds, and gives up five seconds after that. A Go test (TestCollectionHookEndsItsGroup) runs a hook whose child ignores SIGTERM past a 300 ms bound: the group is gone when run returns, 5.33 s on; against the released code it fails, the group still there.
