63. The audit trail's names and fields (2026-10-17) #

The ROADMAP's Later item "The audit trail, and then an audit review tool", its first part opened on the operator's word: every audit event named and linked alike in every mode, so that journald itself answers what was run at a device, in which job, and by whom.

The evidence. This host's journal, which the suites and the labs of the last 30 days filled with audit events, and /var/log/syslog, which rsyslog fills from the journal; read on 2026-10-17, the writer the released tree's internal/audit/audit.go. An event is one journald entry: MESSAGE (karvi audit EVENT outcome=OUTCOME), PRIORITY, MESSAGE_ID, SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi, three fields of karvi's own (KARVI_EVENT_NAME, KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID, and KARVI_JOB_ID), and the whole record as JSON in KARVI_AUDIT_JSON; the same JSON line goes to audit.file when one is set. The 30 days held thirteen names: run.started 51,411, run.completed 46,035, run.exercised 5,340, run.cancel_requested 1,988, command.started 29,404, command.completed 29,391, command_completed 170,844, crun.after.succeeded 578, crun.after.failed 373, login.started 4,505, login.completed 2,527, login.errored 1,969, and test 228. A run of two devices, a command, and a cancelled run, each by its ID:

$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID=261016-085318-00 -o cat
karvi audit run.started outcome=started
karvi audit command_completed outcome=succeeded
karvi audit command_completed outcome=succeeded
karvi audit run.completed outcome=completed
$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID=261016-085457-00 -o cat
karvi audit command.started outcome=started
karvi audit command_completed outcome=succeeded
karvi audit command.completed outcome=completed
$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID=261016-085239-00 -o cat
karvi audit run.started outcome=started
karvi audit run.cancel_requested outcome=informational
karvi audit command_completed outcome=cancelled
karvi audit command_completed outcome=cancelled
karvi audit command_completed outcome=cancelled
karvi audit command_completed outcome=cancelled
karvi audit run.completed outcome=cancelled

What the entries hold:

  • command_completed is one event per command per device, in every mode, and not the command's end; its JSON names no mode. The run's two are its two devices, 127.0.0.1 and 127.0.0.2, named in the JSON alone; the cancelled run's four are its two devices' two commands, never sent.

  • A collection's job is run.* (261016-085458-00: run.started, command_completed, run.completed, crun.after.succeeded), where job list calls it crun. An --exercise job ends in run.exercised, with no run.completed.

  • A command's events carry KARVI_JOB_ID empty, all 29,404 starts and 52,822 of the command_completed events; their ID, the one job list shows, is in KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID alone. A command's summary and records carry job_id empty too, its folder's name its only job ID. A login has no job, its ID in KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID.

  • The device is in the JSON alone, as device.canonical_name, and a login's as device.name. No field matches it; reading every event's JSON found 21,399 of the 95,946 events of seven days naming fake-iosxe, in 4.8 seconds:

    $ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_DEVICE=fake-iosxe -o cat | wc -l
0

  • A run.started names no device: details.device_count and action.selector_digest.

  • A command is action.command_sha256, which only a guess names; a command_completed of 261016-085459-00 held cb75924d…:

    $ printf 'show clock' | sha256sum
cb75924da5e7bb871e288717e54dc1eb5065c55e8ab1a974be3319cc7f4cd590  -

  • Syslog receives the message alone:

    $ grep -c 'karvi audit' /var/log/syslog
71566
$ grep -m1 'karvi audit command_completed' /var/log/syslog
2026-10-11T06:51:09.848576-04:00 dev karvi[1867301]: karvi audit command_completed outcome=authentication_error

What it gains. An operator on a NOC shift asks journald, or the syslog a host forwards it to, what was run at a device in the last hours, by every operator and service account, a run under --nof included, and reads the operator, the statement, the job, and the device on each line, by name on every host; the events of one mode compare with another's word for word.

What it waits on. Nothing: every event is written today. The audit schema moves from 1 to 2; issue 7 moves the command record's, the job summary's, and the scoreboard's.

Its issues, one at a time: the names; the link to the job; the device's field; the statements in place of the digests; the operator's name; the line's form; the outcome's words; the mask.

Issue 1, the names, agreed. The rule. Every audit event is named <kind>.<event>. The kind is the job's kind as job list shows it, cmd, run, or crun (the summary's kind), or login; action.mode holds the same word in every event. The events: start and end, once each per job or login; command, once per device per command, in place of command_completed; cancel, when a cancel is asked; after, a collection's crun.after hook. An --exercise job ends in <kind>.end with the outcome exercise; a login ends in login.end with the outcome complete or error; the hook is crun.after with the outcome success or fail (the words issue 7's). The outcome is in its own field alone, never in the name. Why: one word per mode across the summary, job list, and the audit, and the same event words in every mode, so that run.end and cmd.end compare as run.command and cmd.command do; each job and each login has one start and one end. Not taken: cmd.completed for the per-command event (one name for a cmd job's end and for every device command of every job, the 29,391 and the 170,844 events of the 30 days under one match); command.completed for it (free once the mode is cmd, but a journal kept across the change would hold both meanings); command_completed kept (the one name with an underscore, and no mode); the past-tense words (started, completed, exercised, cancel_requested); a collection's job named run; the outcome in the name (login.errored, crun.after.failed).

Issue 2, the link to the job, agreed. The rule. Every event of a job, its start, each command, a cancel, its end, and crun.after, carries KARVI_JOB_ID, the ID job list shows, a cmd job's included; a login's events carry KARVI_LOGIN_ID, the ID of its row in watch. KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID leaves journald, and the JSON follows: job_id on a job's events, login_id on a login's, no activity_id. The message names the job (job=ID) or the login (login=ID), and the device where the event has one (device=NAME), in the line issue 6 sets. Why: journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_JOB_ID=ID gives a job's whole trail in order; a login takes its ID from another sequence (the scoreboard folder's) than a job (the output root's), so one field for both would match a login by a job's ID; on every job event the activity ID repeated the job ID, and nothing read it; a forwarder that sends the message alone still links each line. Not taken: KARVI_ACTIVITY_ID kept as the one link (the ID the operator sees is the job's); a login's ID in KARVI_JOB_ID.

Issue 3, the device's field, agreed. The rule. Every <kind>.command event, and a login's login.start and login.end, carries KARVI_DEVICE, the device's canonical name: its inventory name, lowercase, or a direct target as given. The JSON names the device device.canonical_name in every event, a login's device.name renamed. A job's start, cancel, and end, and crun.after, carry none. Why: journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi KARVI_DEVICE=NAME answers what was run at a device, by every operator and service account, a run under --nof included; every selected device has at least one command event, a cancelled or never attempted one included (the cancelled run above), so a job's command events name its every device; and journald matches a field whole, with its case, so the name is the one job list shows. Not taken: KARVI_DEVICE on a job's start, one value per device (2,500 values in one entry for the fleet); a KARVI_ADDRESS field for the address karvi connected to (on the operator's word; the address stays in the JSON, device_identity.selected_address).

Issue 4, the statements in place of the digests, agreed. The rule. The audit records no digest. A <kind>.command event carries its statement as sent: action.command in the JSON, and command="…" in the message. A job's start carries its statements in order, action.commands; no other job event repeats them. action.command_sha256, action.command_sha256_array, action.selector_digest, action.plan_digest, policy.config_digest, and the empty command lists of a login's and crun.after's events are removed. Host-key fingerprints and plan_id stay: they name a key and a plan, and are no digest of karvi's output. In the audit alone, the value after a platform's secret word is masked, by a list the platform definition holds, built in for cisco_iosxe; the job's folder keeps the statements as written. Why: a digest answers what was run only to someone who guesses it, and the message is what rsyslog forwards. The audit is read more widely than a job's folder: on this host the journal's files are root:systemd-journal 0640 with an access list and /var/log/syslog is syslog:adm 0640, besides whatever the host forwards to, where the folder is its operator's or the team's (the reason the scoreboard names no statement, docs/DESIGN.md, section 13); a configuration statement can carry a secret in clear (snmp-server community, a type 0 password, key 0), which IOS XE's own configuration logger masks too (archive log config with hidekeys). Not taken: the digests kept beside the statements (nothing reads them); the statements in clear under the operator's rule alone, as --expect's responses are in the plan (the audit reaches syslog and whatever it forwards to); the statements repeated on end and cancel (the start holds them). The list's key, its built-in words, and the mask are issue 8's.

Issue 5, the operator's name, agreed. The JSON names the operator (operator.username, beside the UID and the groups), journald's own _UID the process's account by number; a UID is a host's, the same operator's differing from host to host, so a central log searched by name finds nothing in _UID. The name is the password database's for the process's UID (user.Current()), a daemon's job taking the daemon's own, and the daemon refuses a client of another UID. 344,156 events of the 30 days named netops beside _UID 1000; the only events with no name were the tests'. Under sudo, 72 events ran as netops.test from a netops login: their name was netops.test, and the person who logged in was journald's _AUDIT_LOGINUID=1000 alone, the kernel's login UID, which sudo keeps. The rule. Every event names its operator: KARVI_OPERATOR=NAME in journald and operator=NAME in the line, NAME the account the job or the login ran as. When the kernel's login UID names another account, KARVI_LOGINUSER=NAME and loginuser=NAME name it too; with no login UID, as for the service account's daemon under systemd, they are absent. A job through the daemon takes its client's login UID, which the daemon reads from the client's process (/proc/PID/loginuid, the PID the socket's peer credentials give), never its own, which is the login of whoever launched it. Why: a SIEM matches an operator by name across hosts; on a jump box where operators sudo to a shared or role account, the shared name alone hides the person. Not taken: _UID alone (a host's number); the login user on every event (it repeats the operator's); the login UID the client reports (the kernel's word over the client's).

Issue 6, the line's form, agreed. The rule. The message is one line of key=value pairs, in this order: karvi.audit=<kind>.<event>; operator=NAME; loginuser=NAME when it differs; outcome=WORD, which a start and a cancel leave out; job=ID or login=ID; device=NAME on <kind>.command, login.start, and login.end; and command="…" on <kind>.command alone, quoted always with " and \ escaped, so that a statement holding spaces, =, or quotes stays one value, and masked as issue 8 masks it. The first key keeps its dot. The form, its values illustrative:

karvi.audit=run.start operator=netops job=261016-085318-00
karvi.audit=run.command operator=netops outcome=success job=261016-085318-00 device=core-rtr-1 command="show clock"
karvi.audit=run.end operator=netops outcome=complete job=261016-085318-00
karvi.audit=login.end operator=noc loginuser=jsmith outcome=error login=261017-101500-00 device=core-rtr-1

Why: one key=value rule reads the whole line, and Splunk extracts the pairs without one; the first key tells an audit line from the daemon's log, which reaches journald under the same identifier and is key=value too (time=… level=INFO msg=request …); and it carries karvi's name, so a line stands alone where another source's audit field would meet it, or where the syslog tag is dropped (journalctl -o cat). Not taken: karvi audit <kind>.<event> (bare words, a parser rule per source); the name bare after it (karvi audit netops run.command …); audit= (another source's field); karvi_audit= (some read the dot as nesting, Elasticsearch an audit under karvi; kept on the operator's word).

Issue 7, the outcome's words, agreed. An event's outcome is a word karvi's records already hold: a command event's is the device record's status (commands.jsonl, the summary's devices, job list --target's OUTCOME), a job's end the summary's final_status (job list's and watch's STATUS). The 30 days held started, completed, errored, cancelled, halted, incomplete, exercised, not_ready, informational, succeeded, failed, and the device statuses from device_error to not_attempted_prior_command_failure. The rule. An outcome or a status that is a past tense becomes one present-tense word, alike in every record karvi writes, the command record, the summary, the scoreboard, job list, watch, and the audit: succeeded success, completed complete, errored error, failed fail, cancelled cancel, halted halt, exercised exercise, and started start; incomplete, timeout, not_ready, and the *_error words stay. The compound causes with a past tense inside (not_attempted_prior_command_failure, not_started_halt, output_limit_exceeded, incomplete_shutdown, and their like) wait for item 20's review of the output strings. A start and a cancel carry no outcome. The command record's schema moves from 3 to 4, the job summary's from 4 to 5, and the scoreboard's from 3 to 4. The section that builds it lists every such word first for the operator's review, the counts named after outcomes (device_counts, the scoreboard's) and the collection's replaced and kept among them. Why: one word for one outcome wherever an operator reads it, the audit beside job list; a start's outcome repeated its name, and a cancel's said informational. Not taken: the audit translating its words alone (complete in the audit and completed in job list for one job); the compound causes shortened now (forms like not_attempt_…; item 20 shortens them whole).

Issue 7's list, agreed. S3 listed every past-tense word karvi writes as an outcome, a status, or a count named after one, and the operator agreed it whole. The rule's eight words change wherever they stand: succeeded (the command record's status, the summary's devices[].outcome, the scoreboard's targets[].state, job list --target's OUTCOME, the audit's <kind>.command and crun.after), completed and errored (the summary's final_status, the scoreboard's status, job list's and watch's STATUS, the audit's <kind>.end, a login's status and login.end), failed (where succeeded stands but in the command record and its event), cancelled (in every one of them), halted (where completed stands but a login's), exercised (where halted stands, and the plan report's outcome); started stood nowhere once S1 left a start without an outcome. Beyond the eight:

  • The counts named after outcomes, the summary's device_counts and the scoreboard's counts, take their outcomes' words: success, fail, cancel. Their completed counts the devices at an end, whatever the outcome, and is job list's DONE: it becomes done, since complete would read as the job's success. total, not_started, incomplete, and in_flight stay.
  • The collection's replaced and kept (the summary's collection, its counts and each device's outcome, the scoreboard's collection, the display's <replaced> and <kept>, crun.after's details) become replace and keep, the counts named alike; the hook's environment, found while building, follows on the operator's word: KARVI_CRUN_REPLACE and KARVI_CRUN_KEEP.
  • The ping gate's counts in the summary's ping.devices, proceeded, degraded, skipped, and capability_failed, count the record's ping.decision and take its words: proceed, proceed_degraded, skip, capability_unavailable; gated, every device the gate saw, names no outcome and stays. The display's ping line says proceed or skip, where it said proceeding or skipped.
  • The plan report's outcome takes plan for planned, so that one field holds one tense (plan, invalid, exercise, not_ready); its readiness and binding states (planned, deferred, bound, unresolved, resolution_failed, deferred_to_exercise_or_live_prepare) are planning states, no outcome, and wait for item 20.

What stays: unfinished, job list's word for a job not yet at its end, a state as incomplete is; the scoreboard's metrics.finished, a count of the devices timed; the error registry's codes and the halt reasons drawn from them (a record's error.code cancelled, the summary's halt.run_wide and terminal_causes halt:cancelled, the audit's result.reason), item 20's with every *_failed code, so that a cancelled record reads status: cancel beside error.code: cancelled; job list --failed, an option; the daemon's log and karvi-prune's report, outside the records the rule names; and the compound causes, as the rule has them. The command record's schema moves to 4, the job summary's to 5, the scoreboard's to 4 (its schema file, which said 2 and left out metrics.in_flight_bytes, corrected with it), and the plan report's to 3. Found on the way: the display gives a <status> value the success role only when it holds success or completed, so a record's succeeded showed in the error role; success and complete take it now.

Issue 8, the mask; first, its form, its stand-in, and where it applies, agreed. The evidence: oxidized (github.com/ytti/oxidized, master at 2cac3f7, 2026-10-09), which backs up network devices' configurations, hides their secrets by a cmd :secret block per model, Ruby substitutions over a command's whole output, each keeping the words before a secret as \1 and writing <secret hidden> after them, or <configuration removed> over the rest of the line. IOS XE takes the IOS model (IOSXE = IOS), 25 rules; NX-OS has 7, EOS 10, IOS XR 2, and Junos 4, three of them on Junos's own ## SECRET-DATA tag in show configuration. They run only when a site sets remove_secret: true, its documents saying "Removing secrets reduces the usefulness as a full configuration backup". Dropping a line is another mechanism (reject_lines): IOS's are ntp clock-period and Current configuration, lines cisco_iosxe's crun-filters drop too; Junos's are none. IOS XE's own configuration logger hides secrets as well (archive log config with hidekeys), its guide naming neither the words nor what it prints in their place. The 25 IOS rules, ported to Go (each with (?m), ${1} for \1; every one compiles), hid every secret of a configuration excerpt as the device prints it, and in 3 of 13 statements sent alone; the port's output, not karvi's:

  sent       "snmp-server comm Publ1c RO"
  unchanged  "snmp-server comm Publ1c RO"

  sent       "key 0 T4cacsKey"
  unchanged  "key 0 T4cacsKey"

  sent       "username ops secret Cl3arPw"
  unchanged  "username ops secret Cl3arPw"

  sent       "snmp-server user mon grp v3 auth sha AuthPw1 priv aes 128 PrivPw1"
  unchanged  "snmp-server user mon grp v3 auth sha AuthPw1 priv aes 128 PrivPw1"

The rules are written for the form the device prints: a submode's line indented (^( +key-string)), a tacacs server's key below its parent line, every word whole and a type digit always, and no rule for a secret the device never prints (IOS's SNMPv3 user's passwords). A statement comes alone and unindented, perhaps abbreviated, and a type 0 value perhaps with no digit, the value in clear.

The rule, amending issue 4's. A platform's mask list holds Go regular expressions; in a statement, every capturing group of every match is replaced by <removed>. A pattern that does not compile, or holds no group, refuses the configuration before any device is contacted. The mask applies to every statement the audit records, in journald and audit.file alike, and never to the job's folder (commands.jsonl and the output); a collection's file takes it only when the site turns it on, off by default. The list is its own key, beside crun-filters, which still drops lines from the collection file alone. cisco_iosxe, cisco_iosxr, cisco_nxos, juniper_junos, and arista_eos each have a built-in list, in force by default, oxidized's rules its start and each written for a statement: ^\s* where oxidized has ^ +, the type digit optional, no parent line, the common abbreviations (comm, pass), and the secrets a device never prints; such a rule matches the printed line too, so one list serves the audit and the collection. A site's [platform.NAME] replaces the list whole, and an empty array turns it off. juniper_junos's crun-filters stays empty: oxidized drops no Junos line, and ## Last commit: is the stamp of the configuration's last change, which cisco_iosxe's crun-filters leave in place too. A secret with no word before it, an answer to a Password: prompt sent as its own statement, passes in clear. Why: the precedent crun-filters and oxidized are both regular expressions, so a site writes its own as it would for either; the value in the group, oxidized's rule turned inside out, keeps the list a string array with one compiler and one stand-in, which a reader searches as one word; the audit is read more widely than the job's folder (issue 4), and a collection is the device's backup, whose restore needs its secrets and which sits in the operator's or the team's folder; a pattern that misses puts a secret into syslog, where one too wide hides a word of the record. Not taken: a list of words, karvi matching each by its abbreviations of three letters or more and masking the word after it (run beside the regular expressions on 13 statements, it caught username ops pass 0 Cl3arPw, which a pattern catches only by spelling the prefix, but hid words of no secret, chain in key chain OSPF-KEYS and generate in crypto key generate rsa, and took seven phrases for one SNMPv3 rule); oxidized's rules as they stand (3 of 13 statements); oxidized's form, a pattern and a replacement per rule (a list of pairs, a stand-in per rule); the mask in crun-filters (a statement a drop pattern matched would leave the audit whole); <secret hidden> and <configuration removed> (two stand-ins, the second hiding an SNMP community's RO and its ACL too); the collection masked by default (a backup without its secrets).

Issue 8, continued: the names, agreed. The rule. A platform's mask list is masks, a string array in [platform.NAME]; a collection applies it when crun.mask, a boolean in [crun], is true, false by default. The plan carries both: crun.mask in its collection block, as it carries crun.directory, and each target platform's masks, which the audit reads as the collection does. The execution plan's schema moves from 13 to 14, and the registry from 30 to 31. A site writes the list in TOML's single-quoted strings, in which a backslash needs no escape:

[crun]
mask = true

[platform.cisco_iosxe]
masks = ['(?i)^\s*snmp-server comm\S* (\S+)']

Why: one short word with no hyphen, beside the table's hyphenated crun-filters, crun-commands, and paging-commands, that names what the list does in the audit and in the collection alike; crun.mask beside directory, directory-mode, and file-mode; both in the plan, as crun-filters and crun.directory are, so that a job run by the daemon masks as one run without it. Not taken: audit-masks (the list serves the collection too); secrets (the list holds patterns, not secrets, and the property screen of the audit and the plan report, executionplan.SensitivePropertyPattern, refuses any name holding secret: run on the candidates, it refused secrets and secret_masks, and passed masks).

Issue 8, continued: cisco_iosxe's list, agreed. Nineteen patterns, oxidized's rules their start, each written for a statement: a command's no form, the type digit optional, the abbreviations snmp-s…, comm…, pass…, and sec… (other keywords whole), and, beyond oxidized's, an SNMPv3 user's two passwords, the password-encrypt master key, NHRP's key, and a URL's password (copy … scp://ops:pw@host/…). A scratch check ran them over 63 statements as sent, 49 of them holding a secret, and over a configuration of 46 lines as the device prints it, each line naming its secrets: no secret was left in place, and two words of no secret were removed; the check's output, not karvi's:

over  sent   "description uplink to core, password reset by noc"
      after  "description uplink to core, password <removed> by noc"
over  line   " key 1"
      after  " key <removed>"

The rule. cisco_iosxe's built-in masks is the list below. Every pattern is found on the statement as sent, and text that more than one group covers is replaced once. The two words removed stand. The password rule leaves password encryption aes, which IOS XE prints once type 6 is on, whole: encryption is an alternative holding no group, which Go's matcher takes first where it matches (found while drafting cisco_nxos's list; the list first agreed removed the word). Why: a description says anything; the key chain's key ID key 1 falls to the bare key rule that catches key T4cacsKey under tacacs server. Not taken: that rule narrowed to a type digit or a value beginning with a letter (a clear key that begins with a digit would pass); more abbreviations (each widens a pattern beyond the keyword's own; a keyword abbreviated otherwise passes, as a secret with no word before it does).

masks = [
  # SNMP: community, a host's v1/v2c community, a v3 user's auth and priv
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+comm\S*\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+host\s+\S+(?:\s+vrf\s+\S+)?(?:\s+(?:informs?|traps?))?(?:\s+version\s+(?:1|2c|3\s+\S+))?\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bauth\s+(?:md5|sha\S*(?:\s+\d{3})?)\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bpriv\s+(?:des\S*|3des|aes(?:\s+\d{3})?)\s+(\S+)',
  # password or secret anywhere: username, enable (with level), line, BGP
  # neighbor, PPP, IS-IS, dot1x; abbreviations pass… and sec…; encryption
  # holds no secret
  '(?i)\b(?:pass(?:w(?:o(?:r(?:d)?)?)?)?|sec(?:r(?:e(?:t)?)?)?)\s+(?:encryption\s|(?:level\s+\d+\s+)?(?:\d\s+)?(\S+))',
  '(?i)\bpassword-encrypt\s+(\S+)',
  # keys: tacacs/radius server's bare key, legacy -server key, server-key and
  # pac key, ISAKMP, IKEv2 pre-shared and pre-share, OSPF and NTP, key chains
  # and HSRP key-string
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?key\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)\s*$',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?(?:tacacs|radius)-server\s.*?\bkey\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:server-key|pac\s+key)\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?crypto\s+isakmp\s+key\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bpre-shared-key\s+(?:(?:local|remote)\s+)?(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bpre-share\s+key\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bauthentication-key\s+(?:\d+\s+)?(?:(?:md5|sha\S*|cmac\S*|hmac\S*)\s+)?(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bmessage-digest-key\s+\d+\s+md5\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bkey-string\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  # HSRP and VRRP plain text, wireless PSK, NHRP, a URL's password
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?(?:standby|vrrp)\s+\d+\s+authentication\s+(?:text\s+)?(\S+)\s*$',
  '(?i)\b(?:wpa-psk|set-key)\s+(?:ascii|hex)\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bnhrp\s+authentication\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:ftp|tftp|scp|sftp|https?)://[^/\s:@]+:([^@\s]+)@',
]

Issue 8, continued: cisco_iosxr's list, agreed. Fifteen patterns. IOS XR writes encrypted or clear where IOS XE writes a type digit, and a type of two digits (secret 10 $6$…); its IS-IS lsp-password and hello-password name hmac-md5 or text before the type; HSRP's plain-text key is a bare authentication VALUE line and VRRP's is text-authentication; key-string and pre-shared-key take password before the value. IOS XE's password-encrypt, ISAKMP, pre-share key, pac key, wireless, NHRP, standby or vrrp … authentication, and enable … level have no such form on IOS XR and are left out. The same check ran over 48 statements as sent, 39 of them holding a secret, and over a configuration of 53 lines in IOS XR's printed form, written from its documented syntax and not read from a device: no secret was left in place, and one word of no secret was removed, the key chain's key ID, as on IOS XE:

over  line   " key 1"
      after  " key <removed>"

The rule. cisco_iosxr's built-in masks is the list below. The key ID removed stands, as on IOS XE. A bare authentication line's value is removed when it holds 8 characters or fewer, HSRP's limit, so that OSPF's authentication message-digest stays and authentication null loses its word.

masks = [
  # SNMP: community, a host's community, a v3 user's auth and priv
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+comm\S*\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+host\s+\S+(?:\s+vrf\s+\S+)?(?:\s+(?:informs?|traps?))?(?:\s+version\s+(?:1|2c|3\s+\S+))?(?:\s+(?:encrypted|clear))?\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bauth\s+(?:md5|sha\S*(?:\s+\d{3})?)\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bpriv\s+(?:des\S*|3des|aes(?:\s+\d{3})?)\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear)\s+)?(\S+)',
  # password or secret anywhere: username, BGP and LDP neighbor, IS-IS
  # lsp- and hello-password; abbreviations pass… and sec…
  '(?i)\b(?:pass(?:w(?:o(?:r(?:d)?)?)?)?|sec(?:r(?:e(?:t)?)?)?)\s+(?:(?:hmac-md5|text)\s+)?(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d{1,2})\s+)?(\S+)',
  # keys: a tacacs/radius host's bare key, -server key, server-key, IKEv2,
  # OSPF and NTP, key chains
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?key\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d)\s+)?(\S+)\s*$',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?(?:tacacs|radius)-server\s.*?\bkey\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bserver-key\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bpre-shared-key\s+(?:(?:local|remote)\s+)?(?:(?:clear|password|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bauthentication-key\s+(?:\d+\s+)?(?:(?:md5|sha\S*|hmac\S*)\s+)?(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bmessage-digest-key\s+\d+\s+md5\s+(?:(?:encrypted|clear|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bkey-string\s+(?:(?:clear|password|\d)\s+)?(\S+)',
  # HSRP plain text (8 characters at most), VRRP text, a URL's password
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?authentication\s+(\S{1,8})\s*$',
  '(?i)\btext-authentication\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:ftp|tftp|scp|sftp|https?)://[^/\s:@]+:([^@\s]+)@',
]

Issue 8, continued: cisco_nxos's list, agreed. Thirteen patterns. NX-OS quotes some values (tacacs-server key 7 "…", an LDAP server's password), so a value is a quoted string, taken whole with its spaces, or one word. It prints an SNMPv3 user's keys (auth md5 0x… priv 0x… localizedkey), priv taking aes-128 before the value; a host's community is the word after traps or informs, so that snmp-server host … use-vrf management stays; and snmp-server mib community-map names a community too. Its password lines that hold no secret, no password strength-check, password secure-mode, and feature password encryption aes, stay whole by alternatives holding no group, which Go's matcher takes first. It has no tacacs server submode, so the bare key rule is left out, and with it the key ID removed; ISAKMP, IKEv2, NHRP, and wireless are left out too; PIM's hello-authentication ah-md5 and HSRP's and VRRP's authentication text are added. The same check ran over 41 statements as sent, 28 of them holding a secret, and over a configuration of 36 lines in NX-OS's printed form, written from its documented syntax and not read from a device: no secret was left in place, and no word of no secret was removed. The rule. cisco_nxos's built-in masks is the list below.

masks = [
  # SNMP: community, a host's community after traps or informs, the MIB
  # community map, a v3 user's auth and priv (printed as localized keys too)
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+comm\S*\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+host\s+\S+\s+(?:informs|traps)(?:\s+version\s+(?:1|2c|3\s+\S+))?\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+mib\s+community-map\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bauth\s+(?:md5|sha\S*)\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bpriv\s+(?:aes-128\s+)?(\S+)',
  # password or secret anywhere: username, enable, BGP neighbor, LDAP;
  # strength-check, secure-mode, and encryption hold no secret
  '(?i)\b(?:pass(?:w(?:o(?:r(?:d)?)?)?)?|sec(?:r(?:e(?:t)?)?)?)\s+(?:strength-check|secure-mode|encryption\s|(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+))',
  # keys: tacacs/radius, OSPF and NTP, key chains and HSRP key-string
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?(?:tacacs|radius)-server\s.*?\bkey\s+(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)\bauthentication-key\s+(?:\d+\s+)?(?:(?:md5|sha\S*)\s+)?(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)\bmessage-digest-key\s+\d+\s+md5\s+(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)\bkey-string\s+(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  # HSRP and VRRP text, PIM hello, a URL's password
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?authentication\s+text\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)\bhello-authentication\s+ah-md5\s+(?:\d\s+)?("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:ftp|tftp|scp|sftp|https?)://[^/\s:@]+:([^@\s]+)@',
]

Issue 8, continued: arista_eos's list, agreed. Thirteen patterns. EOS writes sha512 as a type word. Its password rule takes password or secret as a word alone, so that session shared-secret profile PROF stays (EOS's IS-IS has no area-password), and leaves management security's password minimum …, password policy …, and password encryption-key … whole by alternatives holding no group; a shared-secret profile's secret 1 7 KEY receive-lifetime … loses KEY alone, by an alternative before the general one. SNMPv3 takes sha to sha512 and des, 3des, and aes to aes256; in the printed form, localized ENGINEID auth sha 0x… priv aes 0x…, the engine ID stays, since it names the engine and is no secret, where oxidized hides it. IS-IS's authentication key, VRRP's peer authentication text and ietf-md5 key-string, and a MACsec profile's key CKN 7 CAK are masked, the CAK alone, the CKN an ID; service unsupported-transceiver NAME KEY loses the key alone, where oxidized removes the tail; the URL rule takes EOS's scp: with or without //. The bare key rule (EOS has no tacacs server submode), HSRP, ISAKMP, IKEv2, NHRP, and wireless are left out. The same check ran over 43 statements as sent, 32 of them holding a secret, and over a configuration of 46 lines in EOS's printed form, written from its documented syntax and not read from a device: no secret was left in place, and no word of no secret was removed. The rule. arista_eos's built-in masks is the list below.

masks = [
  # SNMP: community, a host's community, a v3 user's auth and priv
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+comm\S*\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+host\s+\S+(?:\s+vrf\s+\S+)?(?:\s+(?:informs?|traps?))?(?:\s+version\s+(?:1|2c|3\s+\S+))?\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bauth\s+(?:md5|sha\d{0,3})\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?snmp-s\S*\s+user\s.*?\bpriv\s+(?:des|3des|aes\d{0,3})\s+(\S+)',
  # password or secret as a word: username, enable, aaa root, BGP neighbor,
  # a shared-secret profile's key; management security's minimum, policy,
  # and encryption-key hold no secret
  '(?i)(?:^|\s)(?:pass(?:w(?:o(?:r(?:d)?)?)?)?|sec(?:r(?:e(?:t)?)?)?)\s+(?:minimum\s|policy\s|encryption\S*\s|\d+\s+\d\S*\s+(\S+)\s+receive-lifetime|(?:(?:\d|sha512)\s+)?(\S+))',
  # keys: tacacs/radius, OSPF and NTP, IS-IS and VRRP, key-string, MACsec CAK
  '(?i)^\s*(?:no\s+)?(?:tacacs|radius)-server\s.*?\bkey\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bauthentication-key\s+(?:\d+\s+)?(?:(?:md5|sha\S*)\s+)?(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bmessage-digest-key\s+\d+\s+md5\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bauthentication\s+(?:key|text)\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)\bkey-string\s+(?:\d\s+)?(\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*key\s+[0-9a-f]+\s+\d\s+(\S+)',
  # the licence key, a URL's password
  '(?i)\bunsupported-transceiver\s+\S+\s+(\S+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:ftp|tftp|scp|sftp|https?):(?://)?[^/\s:@]+:([^@\s]+)@',
]

Issue 8, continued: juniper_junos's list, agreed. Ten patterns. Junos tags each secret line of its printed form itself, "…"; ## SECRET-DATA, and one rule, oxidized's, removes the value before the tag; a set statement carries no tag, so the others name each keyword: encrypted-password, plain-text-password-value, authentication-password, privacy-password, simple-password, privacy-key, secret, authentication-key, md5 N key, and pre-shared-key ascii-text or hexadecimal, each serving both forms. A value is quoted, taken whole with its spaces, or one word without the ;. The community is the secret: after snmp community, as v3's community-name, or a printed community NAME { block, so that a policy's community CUST members … stays. NTP's authentication-key 1 type md5 value V loses V, not the key's number, by an alternative before the general one; system login password minimum-length 8, format sha512, and the printed password { stay whole by alternatives holding no group; oxidized's archive-site rule covers a URL's password, pasvftp among the schemes. A bare plain-text-password holds no value, Junos asking for it at a prompt, and so falls under the recorded limit, as Junos's abbreviations do. The same check ran over 33 set statements, 22 of them holding a secret, and over a show configuration of 94 lines in Junos's hierarchical form, written from its documented syntax and not read from a device: no secret was left in place, and no word of no secret was removed. The rule. juniper_junos's built-in masks is the list below. The printed form follows Junos's own tag, so that an SSH public key, which Junos tags, is removed there, as oxidized removes it, and kept in a statement, since a public key is no secret. Not taken: an exception to the tag for SSH keys (a rule beside Junos's own word on what is secret).

masks = [
  # the printed form: Junos tags each secret line itself
  '(?i)\s("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+);\s*## SECRET-DATA',
  # SNMP: the community in a statement, v3's community-name, a printed block
  '(?i)\bsnmp\s+community\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)',
  '(?i)^\s*community\s+("[^"]*"|\S+)\s*\{',
  '(?i)\bcommunity-name\s+("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+)',
  # authentication-key (BGP, IS-IS, VRRP, v3), NTP's value first
  '(?i)\bauthentication-key\s+(?:\d+\s+type\s+\S+\s+value\s+("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+)|("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+))',
  # passwords and secrets: login, v3 users, OSPF simple, RADIUS, TACACS+,
  # key chains; login password rules and a printed block hold no secret
  '(?i)\b(?:encrypted-password|plain-text-password-value|authentication-password|privacy-password|simple-password|privacy-key|secret)\s+("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+)',
  '(?i)\bpassword\s+(?:(?:minimum|maximum)-\S+\s|format\s|change-type\s|[{;]|("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+))',
  # OSPF MD5, IKE, a URL's password
  '(?i)\bmd5\s+\d+\s+key\s+("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+)',
  '(?i)\bpre-shared-key\s+(?:ascii-text|hexadecimal)\s+("[^"]*"|[^\s;]+)',
  '(?i)\b(?:ftp|pasvftp|tftp|scp|sftp|https?)://[^/\s:@"]+:([^@\s"]+)@',
]

Issue 8, continued: a job's events, agreed. A job sends the same statements to every device, so that a device's events masked by its own platform's list alone would leave in clear what another platform's list hides. A job across cisco_iosxe, juniper_junos, and linux, its statements show clock, snmp-server community Publ1c RO, and set snmp community Publ1c authorization read-only, each device's events masked by its own list and by the lists of all the job's platforms; a scratch check's output, not karvi's:

  core-rtr-1 cisco_iosxe   own list   "set snmp community Publ1c authorization read-only"   <- in clear
  core-rtr-1 cisco_iosxe   all lists  "set snmp community <removed> authorization read-only"
  edge-1     juniper_junos own list   "snmp-server community Publ1c RO"   <- in clear
  edge-1     juniper_junos all lists  "snmp-server community <removed> RO"
  srv-1      linux         own list   "snmp-server community Publ1c RO"   <- in clear
  srv-1      linux         all lists  "snmp-server community <removed> RO"

The rule. Every audit event of a job, its start and each device's command events, the session-init statements among them, is masked by the plan's masks of every target platform together; a job whose devices share one platform is masked by that platform's list alone. A collection's file, under crun.mask = true, is masked by its device's own platform's list. A device on linux in a job across platforms takes the network platforms' lists; a job on linux alone has none unless the site sets [platform.linux] masks. Why: no list leaves a statement in clear in any event of the job, and the cost falls on a job across platforms alone: every platform's statements masked by all five lists left no secret in place, and removed words the platform's own list keeps on 14 of cisco_iosxe's 63 statements, 20 of cisco_iosxr's 48, 13 of cisco_nxos's 41, 13 of arista_eos's 43, and 5 of juniper_junos's 33, most of them type words (0, clear, aes, sha512) and some a word one list keeps and another removes (NX-OS's strength-check, EOS's minimum and profile, Junos's format); a collection's file is its device's own printed form, which another platform's rules would read wrongly. Not taken: each device's events by its own list and the start alone by all (the lines in clear above); every job by all five built-in lists (words removed in every job).

Issue 8 is settled; S4 builds it.

Issue 8, continued while building S4: crun.mask in the plan, agreed. The names' rule had the plan carry crun.mask in its collection block, as it carries crun.directory. The plan's configuration block already carries every key, and since chapter 47 (1feebad) a job reads from it each key the plan only copied, crun.file-mode among them; crun.directory stays in the collection block because the client resolves it. A crun through the daemon under --set crun.mask=true, the lab script's report of the job's manifest and the collection file, not karvi's output:

plan.output.collection  {"directory":"/dev/shm/karvi-s4/lab/cd","word":"crun"}
cd/fake-iosxe           ! snmp-server community <removed> RO

The rule, amending the names'. The plan carries platform_masks, each target platform's list, and no field for crun.mask: the job reads the key from the plan's configuration block, as it reads crun.file-mode, so that a job run by the daemon masks its collection as one run without it. Why: one source for the key, and no plan field that copies one. Not taken: a mask boolean in the collection block (a copy of a key, of the kind chapter 47 removed).

Issue 8, continued while building S4: the collections crun.mask covers, agreed. A run or command given --cd writes one file per device into a collection directory as a crun does; crun-filters are a crun's alone, since they quiet a nightly diff and a run's file says what the device said. A run --cd under each value, then a site's file holding crun.mask = true and a one-off --set crun.mask=false; the lab scripts' report of the file's marker line, not karvi's output:

run --cd, crun.mask=false              ! snmp-server community Publ1c RO
run --cd, crun.mask=true               ! snmp-server community <removed> RO
crun, the site's crun.mask = true      ! snmp-server community <removed> RO
crun, --set crun.mask=false            ! snmp-server community Publ1c RO

The rule. crun.mask = true masks every collection file: a crun's, and a run's or command's given --cd. An operator who needs one job's file whole writes --set crun.mask=false for that invocation, unless the site has locked the key: crun.mask is lock-eligible, and a lock declared in the global file ([config-lock] "crun.mask" = true) refuses the --set with config_lock_violation, as chapter 47's issue 6 shows for another key (the lock was not run here: only the auto-discovered global file may declare one). Why: the mask is about what the directory holds, and a run --cd into it under the site's choice would put secrets back; the one-off is the key's own precedence, and the lock the site's way to forbid it. Not taken: the mask a crun's alone, as the filters are.

Issue 8, continued while building S4: the marker line, agreed. Each block of a collection file begins with ! COMMAND, the statement as sent, which crun-filters never match. A crun of snmp-server community Publ1c RO; the lab script's report of the marker line, not karvi's output:

crun.mask=false   ! snmp-server community Publ1c RO
crun.mask=true    ! snmp-server community <removed> RO

The rule. Under crun.mask = true the marker's statement is masked by the device's own platform's list, as the device's output lines are; under false it stays as sent. The list is matched against the statement, not the whole line, so that a pattern anchored at the start (^\s*…snmp-s…) finds it after the ! . Why: the marker is a line of the file, and a statement there holds a secret as the audit's does. Not taken: the marker whole under the mask (the file would keep a secret the audit hides).

Issue 8, continued while building S4: the code and the plan's name, agreed. A configuration whose mask list holds a bad pattern, karvi's messages:

config_platform_mask_invalid: pattern 2 "(" does not compile: error parsing regexp: missing closing ): `(` for platform.lab_iosxe.masks at --set[1]
config_platform_mask_invalid: pattern 1 "^hostname \\S+" holds no capturing group for platform.lab_iosxe.masks at --set[1]

The rule. A pattern that does not compile or holds no group is refused config_platform_mask_invalid (exit 2, before any device is contacted), beside config_platform_crun_filter_invalid and in its form; the plan carries the lists as platform_masks, beside platform_commands and platform_filters (a job across cisco_iosxe, juniper_junos, and linux carried the first two, linux having none). The plan's check refuses the same two faults under execution_plan_invalid, naming platform_masks. Why: each name beside its precedent's.

Issue 8, continued while building S4: a group that matched no text, agreed. A site's pattern may hold a group that can match nothing, (\S*); none of the five built-in lists does. The mask's unit test, opt(\d*), its cases, not karvi's output:

"opt"     stays    "opt"
"opt12"   becomes  "opt<removed>"

The rule. A group that matched no text is left alone: only text a group covers is replaced by <removed>. Why: the stand-in says text was removed, and where there was none it would say what is not so. Not taken: the stand-in written at an empty group's place.

Found, for later. Three, each after this chapter's build, in this order:

  • The tests write into the host's journal: internal/audit/audit_test.go's 228 test events, internal/app/one_read_test.go's crun.after.succeeded events of a job 261010-120000-00 with no activity ID (81), 112 command_completed events with no operator or ID, and every suite's jobs, the 170,844 command_completed events among them. An audit review would show them as work done.
  • karvi-audit, its shape agreed on the operator's word, chapter 64's: a fourth executable, like karvi-prune, that reads the trail by running journalctl -o json SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi with the matches, so that following, reversing, grepping, and who reads whose events are journalctl's (an operator their own, adm and systemd-journal everyone's), and shows a table: TIME, KIND, EVENT, OPERATOR, OUTCOME, JOB-ID (a job's or a login's), DEVICE, and COMMAND, the command cut at the terminal's width with … and never to a pipe or a file, coloured as karvi's other output (a success green, a warning orange, an error red; never into a file). Its options, by Go's flag package, take one or two dashes and = or a space: -f/-follow, -r/-reverse, -g/-grep PATTERN, -o/-operator NAME (the operator or the login user), -d/-device NAME (lowercased), the last two repeatable and matched whole, with journalctl's -n/-lines, -S/-since, and -U/-until, and karvi's -nocolor; with none, every event, oldest first. Its design opens with a mock-up of the table from real events, laid out by a script.
  • A job ID is unique only in the folder that reserved it: the output root, a collection's --cd folder, or none under --nof, whose ID is always -00. Of the 43,173 job IDs of the 30 days' run.started events, 6,712 were started by more than one process; 261016-085416-00 is a command (pid 3825619) and an exercised run (pid 3825609), the two in the same second, so once a cmd job's events carry KARVI_JOB_ID that ID matches both. The direction: one sequence per operator on a host for every job and login.

Agreed while building S2: a session-init statement. A session-init profile's statements are chosen per device, so a job's start, whose action.commands holds the job's statements, names none of them; each has its own <kind>.command event, told from the job's statements by action.command_kind, session_init or requested, in the JSON alone. A run under a profile sending show clock; the S2 lab script's report of audit.file (audit_events: the event, the job, the kind, the statement, the statements), not karvi's output:

run.command  261017-074223-00  requested     show version

    261017-091934-00  exercise  {"total":1,"done":1,"success":0,"fail":0,"not_started":0,"in_flight":0,"incomplete":0,"cancel":0}  [{"name":"fake-iosxe","state":"queued","bytes":0}]

Executed. 64. karvi-audit, the audit trail as a table (2026-10-17) #

The ROADMAP's Next item 1, opened on the operator's word: a fourth executable, like karvi-prune, that reads the audit trail by running journalctl -o json and shows it as a table, its shape and its options agreed in chapter 63's "Found, for later".

The evidence. A lab build of the tree at 7ffa2ec made 26 events in one window (c0-lab.sh): a cmd; a run of two devices, a masked statement and a long one among its three, dead-iosxe unreachable; a crun with its hook; an exercise; a cancelled run; a login; and a cmd by netops.test under sudo -n -u from the netops login. The daemon's log reaches journald under the same identifier: 23 of the 30 days' entries under SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi carry no MESSAGE_ID, each a line like time=… level=INFO msg=request …, so the reading matches the audit's MESSAGE_ID, 9cb838d10f074d8a928e9f7c2f98450a, too. The host's trail is large: 359,728 events in 30 days, the tests' and the suites' among them, which journalctl -o json --output-fields=KARVI_AUDIT_JSON read in 16 seconds, 552 MB through its pipe, and which a Go reader holding each event's eight cells kept in 157 MB after 18 seconds (c0-rows.go). The lab, the events, and the layouts are kept beside the tree (release-design-evidence/karvi-audit-2026-10-17).

What it gains. An operator, or whoever reviews the operators, reads the trail as a table: what was run, by whom, at which device, in which job, and how it ended, without journalctl's field names, and follows it on a NOC shift.

What it waits on. Nothing: every event is written today. On a host where the tests run, the table shows the tests' events as work done (the ROADMAP's Later item).

Its issues, one at a time: the widths; a terminal narrower than the columns; the operator under sudo; the colours; the run, journalctl missing or refused, nothing matched, an event it cannot read, and the exit statuses.

Issues 1 and 2, the layout, agreed. The rule. No TIME column. The columns, at fixed widths with one space between them: JOB-ID 16 (a job's or a login's ID), OPERATOR 18, MODE 5 (the event's kind: cmd, run, crun, or login), EVENT 7, OUTCOME 16, DEVICE 20, then COMMAND. A cell longer than its column is cut with …. At a terminal the line is cut with … so that at least one cell stays free at its right edge: COMMAND may be cut, or not shown at all; to a pipe or a file nothing cuts the line, and COMMAND is whole. OPERATOR and DEVICE, heading and cells, are centred in their columns, an odd cell to the right, while the width holds the column whole, and at the column's left when the width cuts into it. The cell after DEVICE is kept for the line's …, so DEVICE is whole from 89 columns. The c3-mockup.py script's layout of four of the lab's events at 100 columns, not karvi's output:

JOB-ID                OPERATOR      MODE  EVENT   OUTCOME                 DEVICE        COMMAND
261017-143817-00       netops       cmd   command success               fake-iosxe      show versi…
261017-143818-00       netops       run   command connection_error      dead-iosxe      show clock
261017-143825-00       netops       login start                         fake-iosxe
261017-143828-00 netops.test(netop… cmd   command device_error          fake-iosxe      show ip in…

The same four at 80 columns, DEVICE at its left:

JOB-ID                OPERATOR      MODE  EVENT   OUTCOME          DEVICE     …
261017-143817-00       netops       cmd   command success          fake-iosxe …
261017-143818-00       netops       run   command connection_error dead-iosxe …
261017-143825-00       netops       login start                    fake-iosxe
261017-143828-00 netops.test(netop… cmd   command device_error     fake-iosxe …

Why: the job ID holds the job's start to the second (261017-143817-00), and a login's its own; one rule for every mode, a table read whole or followed under -f, its first line at once and its memory flat, which widths measured over the rows cannot give (the 30 days' 359,728 rows held before the first line, and under -f rows not yet read); OUTCOME at 16 holds 9 of a command's 17 words, device_error and connection_error among them, and tells not_attempted_prior_command_failure from not_attempted_session_init_failure (not_attempted_p…, not_attempted_s…); centred cells read as a column, and a column the width cuts keeps its names whole at its left (fake-iosxe at 80 columns, which centred would be cut). Not taken: TIME (2026-10-17 14:38:17, 19 cells, watch's form); widths measured over every row read, as job list's (c0-mockup.out); fixed widths with a longer cell whole, pushing the rest of its row (c0-mockup-fixed.out, three of the 26 rows out of line); the heading KIND; two cells between columns, as job list's; OUTCOME at 10 (3 of the 17 words, both not_attempted words not_attem…).

Issue 3, the operator under sudo, agreed. The rule. OPERATOR shows the event's operator, the account the job or the login ran as, or OPERATOR/LOGINUSER when the event names a login user, the person behind sudo (chapter 63, issue 5). A pair longer than its 18 cells keeps /LOGINUSER whole and cuts the operator's part with …; a login user too long for that is cut at the pair's end; the layouts of issues 1 and 2 show the pair as it stood before this issue. -o NAME matches either name, as agreed. The c5-operator.py script's layout of the cell, centred, for the lab's two operators and three illustrative pairs, not karvi's output:

operator, loginuser          |     OPERATOR     |
netops, -                    |      netops      |
netops.test, netops          |netops.test/netops|
noc, jsmith                  |    noc/jsmith    |
svc-karvi, jsmith            | svc-karvi/jsmith |
svc-karvi-collector, jsmith  |svc-karvi-…/jsmith|

Why: on a jump box where operators sudo to a shared or role account, the shared name alone hides the person, whom a review looks for, so the person's name is the part kept whole; one cell, one character between the names, so that the lab's netops.test/netops fits its 18. Not taken: OPERATOR(LOGINUSER) (a cell more, the lab's pair cut at 19); the pair cut at its end (the person cut first, netops.test(netop…); the operator alone (the person hidden); a column of its own (the width issue 1 spends).

Issue 4, the colours, agreed. The rule. The headings in the label role (blue in the dark theme), OPERATOR's cells in the accent role (cyan), DEVICE's in the target role (yellow, bold), and OUTCOME's by the word: the success role (green) for success, complete, and exercise; the warning role (orange, bold) for work not done or cut short, cancel, halt, incomplete, and a command's not_attempted_*, not_started_*, and incomplete_*; the error role (red) for every other word, error, fail, and a command's failures (device_error, connection_error, authentication_error, timeout, …). The rest plain. karvi-audit reads no configuration, as karvi-prune: the dark theme's roles, the colour written to a terminal and to a pipe, never into a file; -nocolor and NO_COLOR turn it off. The c7-colour.py script wrote the lab's 26 events at 132 columns in karvi's codes (c7-colour.ansi); two of its rows, the codes shown by cat -v, not karvi's output:

261017-143828-00 ^[[36mnetops.test/netops^[[0m cmd   start
261017-143828-00 ^[[36mnetops.test/netops^[[0m cmd   command ^[[31mdevice_error^[[0m          ^[[1;33mfake-iosxe^[[0m      show ip interface brief

Why: the roles and the words' colours are watch's and job list's (complete and exercise green, cancel and halt orange, error red); a statement not sent is not the failure, which a row before it in the same job carries in red; the operator in the accent reads apart from the device; a reader of the trail pages it (karvi-audit | less -R), so a pipe keeps the colour, and a file never holds it (chapter 56, issue 19). Not taken: the colour at a terminal alone (display.color = auto's rule, the pager plain); not_attempted_* red (one failure shown as many); OPERATOR plain; the configuration's display.* read (the fourth executable reads none, as karvi-prune).

Issue 5, the run, agreed. The rule. karvi-audit runs journalctl --no-pager -o json --output-fields=KARVI_AUDIT_JSON SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi MESSAGE_ID=9cb838d10f074d8a928e9f7c2f98450a with the matches, -S, -U, and -g passed as given and -n a Go integer. It refuses its own options alone: an unknown option, a positional argument, or an -n that is not a number, in few words with the help, exit 2, as karvi-prune. A value journalctl refuses, a time, a pattern, or -r with -f, is journalctl's: its message on standard error as it wrote it, exit 1. journalctl missing is karvi-audit: journalctl not found in red, exit 1. Not following, the heading is printed with the first row, and when journalctl returned no entry, karvi-audit: no matches goes to standard error in orange, with no heading, exit 0; following, the heading first, then each row as it comes. An entry with no KARVI_AUDIT_JSON, JSON that does not decode, or an audit schema other than 2 has no row: at the end, one line on standard error in orange counts them (karvi-audit: N events not shown: not audit schema 2), a follow ended by Ctrl-C included, and when every entry was such, that line alone. The exit is 0 when journalctl ended 0, a follow ended by Ctrl-C or by its reader's closing included; 1 when journalctl is missing or ends otherwise; 2 for a usage error. A reader that quits (less, head) ends it quietly, under -f without waiting for the next event, as journalctl's own follow ends. The c8-run.sh script's report of journalctl in four of the cases, not karvi's output:

$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi MESSAGE_ID=9cb8… -o json --since=yesterdayx
(script) exit 1, stdout 0 lines
    Failed to parse timestamp: yesterdayx
$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi MESSAGE_ID=9cb8… -o json --reverse --follow -n 1
(script) exit 1, stdout 0 lines
    Please specify either --reverse or --follow, not both.
$ journalctl SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=karvi MESSAGE_ID=9cb8… -o json -f -n 1, SIGINT after a second
(script) exit 0
(script) the trail's events by audit schema, and those with no KARVI_AUDIT_JSON
    schema_version: {1: 344592, 2: 15123, 7: 1}
    no KARVI_AUDIT_JSON, by executable: {'?': 12}

Nothing matched, journalctl ended 0 and wrote nothing under -o json; a job's trail by its ID as the pattern (-g 261017-143818-00) gave its 8 events; and netops.test, a member of neither adm nor systemd-journal, read its own events with no hint. Why: journalctl already judges its values and says why in one line, so whose refusal is whose has one rule; a heading with no row reads as a table whose rows were lost, and a message on standard output would be a row to a script reading the pipe; the program's name before the message, as the count line's and karvi-prune's, says which program spoke on a shared standard error; on a host upgraded from v0.31.1 the journal keeps schema 1's events (this host's 344,592), which a window can match alone, so "no matches" would be false there. Not taken: karvi-audit refusing -r with -f itself; the heading alone for nothing matched; (no matches); the message on standard output; a row for an event it cannot read (the old schema's rows in the new table); a warning per such event (this host's 344,605 lines); exit 1 for nothing matched (grep's; journalctl's 0 kept).

The build, in sections, each committed on the operator's word. S1 the command line that karvi-prune and karvi-audit share, out of internal/prune: the synopsis, the help, the tab completion, and the man page's regions from one definition of each executable's flags, karvi-prune's text byte for byte; S2 karvi-audit itself, its options, journalctl's invocation and matches, the rows, the layout, the colours, and the run (issues 1 to 5), with its tests; S3 the fourth executable beside the other three, in the build, the package, the install script, the verifiers, the man pages, the tab completion, and a suite; S4 the closing documents and the full battery.

Agreed while building S2: a follow's heading, and a statement's control characters. The rule. Under -f the heading comes with the first row, or once journalctl has run half a second without ending, so that journalctl's refusal of a value, which it says at its start, stands alone, as it does without -f; issue 5's "following, the heading first" so amended. A statement's control characters, a tab, a newline, an escape, are written in COMMAND as Go writes them in a quoted string (\t, \n, \x1b), so that a row stays one line and its width is its cells. Before the change, -r -f wrote the heading to standard output and then journalctl's refusal. The S2 lab after it (s2-lab.sh, s2-follow-empty.out): a $ line the command run, a (script) line the script's own report, and an indented line karvi-audit's output:

$ karvi-audit -r -f
(script) exit 1, 0 lines out, 1 err
    Please specify either --reverse or --follow, not both.
$ karvi-audit -f -S yesterdayx
(script) exit 1, 0 lines out, 1 err
    Failed to parse timestamp: yesterdayx
$ karvi-audit --nocolor -f -d nosuch, Ctrl-C after 1 s
(script) after 0.3 s: 0 lines
(script) after 1 s: 1 lines
(script) exit 0, standard error 0 bytes

Why: a heading over a refusal reads as a table cut short; journalctl refuses at its start, well inside the half second; an empty follow still shows that it waits. A newline in a statement would start a row with no columns, and a tab or an escape moves the cells after it. Not taken: the heading with the first row under -f too (an empty follow blank until an event); karvi-audit refusing -r with -f itself (issue 5's not taken, and journalctl's other refusals under -f would still follow the heading); the control characters removed, or replaced by a space (the statement as sent no longer shown).

Found while building S2.

  • Ctrl-C reaches journalctl twice, from the terminal and passed on by the reader, and the second can end it by the signal before its own handler ends it 0: the S2 lab's first follow ended by Ctrl-C exited 1. The reader takes a journalctl ended by a signal it got too as the run's end, exit 0.
  • The tree's check on uncoded errors (TestUncodedErrorsAreDetails) refused --lines's own refusal of a word; it says the flag package's words, as karvi-prune --days x does (invalid value "x" for flag -n: parse error), and is listed among the details the check allows.
  • -o matches a name whole, with its case, as journald matches a field: -o NETOPS.TEST matched none of the lab's events; -d alone is lowercased, as a device's canonical name is.

Agreed while building S3: the suite on a host without journald. The rule. The audit suite reads the jobs' events back from the host's journal, the first suite to read journald. With journald, its socket /run/systemd/journal/socket and journalctl, every row runs: the jobs run under audit.journald-required = true, so a journal that takes no event fails karvi itself, and an event not read back within ten seconds fails the suite. Without journald, the reader's own refusals, its help, and journalctl not found still run, then one line says that the journal's rows are skipped and why, and the suite passes, as the canary and v0100 suites skip their ICMP rows on a host without an ICMP method. A copy of the suite whose socket path names none (skip.sh), then the suite itself, on a lab build of the tree with S3's changes: a $ line the command run, a (script) line this report's own, the rest the suite's output:

$ sh skip.sh
audit smoke: j1-j9 SKIP: no journald on this host (/run/systemd/journal/socket, journalctl)
audit smoke: ok
(script) exit 0
$ KARVI=/dev/shm/ka3/bin/karvi ./scripts/audit-smoke-test.sh
audit smoke: ok
(script) exit 0

Why: the suites run wherever the bundle is verified, a container without systemd among them, and a row skipped with its reason is the list's rule for a host that cannot hold it; the rows that need no journal still hold the reader's own run. Not taken: the suite failing on a host without journald (the bundle verifier failing there for the host, not for karvi); a fake journalctl replaying recorded events (the reader's own tests do that; the suite is the round trip through journald); the jobs under journald-required = false (a journal that took no event would read as the reader's fault).

Found while building S3.

  • A job ID names a job in its own output root alone: another suite running beside this one may start a job in the same second under the same ID, so the read by job ID looks for the run's six rows in order among what the pattern matched, not for those rows alone; unique job IDs (the ROADMAP's Next item 2) would make it exact. The run's read, karvi-audit's output kept from the suite's work directory:

    JOB-ID                OPERATOR      MODE  EVENT   OUTCOME                 DEVICE        COMMAND
261017-170821-00       netops       run   start
261017-170821-00       netops       run   command success              up-6015c889      show clock
261017-170821-00       netops       run   command success              up-6015c889      show version
261017-170821-00       netops       run   command connection_error    dead-6015c889     show clock
261017-170821-00       netops       run   command not_attempted_p…    dead-6015c889     show version
261017-170821-00       netops       run   end     error

  • The man page's SYNOPSIS spells a flag as the help does, by its one letter and with ... after a repeatable one, and its OPTIONS gives both spellings (-f, --follow); karvi-prune.8 comes out the same, byte for byte.

  • The release tools' evidence step (evidence-rest.sh, outside the tree) names three executables to go version -m; the release step adds karvi-audit.

Built. In four sections, each committed on the operator's word. 65. The release 0.32.0 (2026-10-17) #

The eleventh public release, 0.32.0, on the operator's word and number, carrying chapter 63 (the audit trail's names, fields, and line; the statements in place of their digests; the mask; the present-tense words; the collection's replace and keep) and chapter 64 (karvi-audit, the fourth executable). Seven counters move: the registry 30 to 31, the execution plan 13 to 14, the command record 3 to 4, the job manifest and summary 4 to 5, the plan report 2 to 3, the scoreboard 3 to 4, and the audit 1 to 2. The daemon IPC schema stays 12, so there is no lifecycle replay and the compatibility example is the drain, beside the released 0.31.1 daemon. The sequence is chapter 62's, the baseline's rule already met: dev held its ## Unreleased block since chapter 63's closing section.

What it gains. A site has the audit trail chapters 63 and 64 made, and karvi-audit to read it, from a published, checksummed bundle and package, with the documents on GitHub Pages at the release: an operator's 0.31.1 daemon is drained by the first submission after the upgrade, and OPERATIONS' upgrade examples are this release's own output.

Before the number. The tree and the release tools were archived first (~/karvi/backup/archive-2026-10-17-2: a mirror at 9b9b12f and the six tools as they were). One tool changed, for the fourth executable: evidence-rest.sh's go version -m line names bin/karvi-audit-linux-amd64 beside the other three. common.sh's prior stays empty. The verifiers already pinned the moved counters, since chapter 63's sections; the number alone changed in them.

The number. VERSION, the Makefile, buildinfo.Version, and the two verifiers; the ## Unreleased block became ## 0.32.0 - 2026-10-17 under a lead paragraph: the seven counters that moved, the rest 0.31.1's, karvi-audit the fourth executable, the module graph 0.31.1's, and what a site changes (a parser of the audit file, the journal, or the syslog it forwards; a script reading the past-tense words or replaced and kept; a display template naming <replaced> or <kept>; a hook reading KARVI_CRUN_REPLACED or KARVI_CRUN_KEPT; a host holding the tab completion file from before). CHECKSUMS.sha256 has four lines.

Where the release lists the executables. release/BUILD-RESULT.md's table has karvi-audit's row, its package line four executables, its suites nineteen with the audit suite, and its build identity the audit counter, which it had not listed; release/release-manifest.json has karvi-audit-linux-amd64 beside the others, with the counters; release/DOWNLOADS.md names four executables in the package; release/evidence/go-version-m.txt the four. The package, the bundle, install.sh, and the verifiers had the executable since chapter 64's S3.

66. One-letter command words, and karvi-audit's DEVICE at 30 (2026-10-18) #

Two changes on the operator's word after the release 0.32.0 (chapter 65), each its own commit: the command words c, r, l, and s, and karvi-audit's DEVICE column at 30 cells.

Issue 1, the one-letter command words. The operator's word: "add aliases for karvi action words, c for command mode, r for run mode, l for login", then "add s as alias for action word stream".

What it gains. One letter for each of the four words an operator types most. The released 0.32.0 refused c (command, config, crun) and s (setup, stream) as ambiguous; r and l reached run and login as prefixes alone, so a word added later beginning with either letter would have made it ambiguous. It waits on nothing: the parser's word rule matches a full name or an alias exactly before any prefix, as it does cmd and -, so each letter is one alias in the table.

The rule, agreed. c, r, l, and s are aliases of command, run, login, and stream, matched exactly as cmd and - are; every other prefix resolves as before, co still ambiguous (command, config) and the only ambiguous one left among the top-level words, cr still crun, se still setup, st still stream. The -c option is unchanged: --cmd after the command word, --config before it. The help and karvi(1) list the letters beside cmd and -, and stream's usage names karvi s; tab completion offers the full words alone, abbreviation reaching the rest as before, and completes a device after c. The parser hands on the canonical word, so a job's kind stays cmd, run, or crun and no record, audit event, or display names a letter.

68. One activity ID for every activity (2026-10-18) #

The operator's review of the ROADMAP's first item, unique job IDs, and the build on the operator's word: every activity takes its ID by one method, so that no two activities share one, the ID's form unchanged; and a cmd job's job_id with it.

The review. The operator judged the risk low and acceptable: two activities must start in one second, and outside shared mode, under --nof, or as a login beside a job; a site concerned can enforce shared mode and tell its staff to avoid --nof. The question was how to take it toward zero with a light fix that keeps the date-and-time form, a central list of IDs in a scratch or persistent folder the proposal to weigh. The code read first: a job that writes files reserved its ID by creating its job directory exclusively under its output root; a login by its scoreboard file, created exclusively; --nof, a dry run, and a login under watch.enabled = false took -00 with nothing behind it. Shared mode puts every operator's job directories in one folder, but left those, a job under --of=PATH, and a login each its own sequence.

What it gains. One ID names one activity: karvi-audit -g ID and journalctl KARVI_JOB_ID=ID find one job, a login's scoreboard is never replaced by a job's, and two runs under --nof through one daemon in one second both run, where the second was refused, the daemon's idempotency key being the job ID. A cmd job's summary, records, and scoreboard name its ID as job_id, which its summary held empty and its records and scoreboard left out. It waits on nothing: the sequence loop and the exclusive create are the job directory's and the login's scoreboard's already.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms: every activity claims its ID once, in one shared folder, before anything else, and the claim is never handed back.

  • Every activity (cmd, run, crun, each run of a stream, a dry run, an exercise, a login) claims its ID first by creating an empty file <ID>.id exclusively in the scoreboards folder: -00 first, the next sequence when the name is taken.
  • A job that writes files also makes its job directory under that ID; both names must be free, or the next sequence is tried.
  • The folder is the scoreboards' chain, whatever watch.enabled says: /dev/shm/karvi/scoreboards in shared mode, one namespace for the host; else the operator's private <basedir>/state/scoreboards.
  • An activity never removes its claim, since a claim released within its second would reopen the ID; each claim removes the operator's own claims of earlier days, the folder being sticky.
  • No setting. A shared folder that cannot be used falls back to the private one with the one orange warning there is today; a claim that cannot be written stops the activity before anything runs, activity_id_generation_failed naming the path and the reason; a site that wants no fallback names the shared folder in scoreboards and locks the key, an explicit path being used or refused.
  • The form stays YYMMDD-HHMMSS-xx; a job's job_id is its ID, a cmd's as a run's.

The first part of the ROADMAP's shorter output strings (item 20), on the operator's word: the six longest of karvi's messages, nominated from a list made by script, each with a shorter form, kept as proposed and built.

What it gains. Six refusals an operator reads in one line, each naming its subject by its value and its fix last, where each took two or three lines of a terminal: 253 to 342 characters with sample values, 130 to 174 after. It waits on nothing: each text sits at its own line of the source, and the code's description already holds what each drops.

The rule, agreed. The 2026-10-13 review's draft, "good thus far" in the operator's words and to be reviewed as the work goes on. In simple terms: say the subject, the fault, and the fix, in few words.

  • The code is not repeated; it leads the line.
  • The subject is named by its value: the key, the path, the device.
  • No word that adds nothing.
  • The reason and the background are the code's description (docs/ERROR-CODES.md), not the message's.
  • A remedy last, after ; , as the operator would type it.
  • Quoting unchanged; values to compare stacked one over the other, two spaces in, coloured per line.
