71. A device as the first word, karvi DEVICE (2026-10-19) #

The operator's request: a first word that would be refused as an unknown command, when it names a target, is a login at it alone, or a command at it with the words after it as the command, "shortcuts for less typing, such as karvi device-name to login at device-name, and karvi router1 show ip int brief which executes command show ip int brief at router1". A target is an exact match in any inventory, a name DNS resolves (a short name by the resolver's search list, router1 as router1.net.example.com at 192.0.2.1), or an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Designed in this session and recorded for the build; the program is unchanged.

What it gains. The two most frequent invocations shorter by their action word: karvi router1 for karvi login router1, karvi router1 show clock for karvi command router1 show clock. It waits on nothing: login and command already resolve a positional device as asked (internal/app/targets.go). A name is matched, ignoring case, against each inventory row's name, canonical name, or ID; any other is a direct target, a literal address its own management address with no lookup, a name looked up in DNS after its name transform by Go's resolver (the executables are built with CGO_ENABLED=0), which applies /etc/resolv.conf's search list. The shortcut is the parser's reading of an unknown first word as one of the two modes, a guard that keeps a mistyped command word from becoming a connection, and the refusals.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms: a first word that is no command and names a target is a login at it, or a command at it when words follow.

  1. Only a first word the parser refuses as unknown (cli_command_unknown) is tried. A command word, an alias, or a unique prefix of one keeps its meaning, and an ambiguous prefix stays cli_command_ambiguous; a device named as one of them is reached by karvi login NAME.
  2. The word is a plain name, one karvi login takes as one literal name: none of * ? [ \ ^ $ and no leading !. Any other word is refused at once as cli_command_unknown, before the configuration is read. A bracketed IPv6 address is a pattern; the plain form, with or without a zone, is an address.
  3. Login or command: the words after the device are read as login's options. It becomes a command at the first word of command text, which with every word after it is the command and never read as options; at -- with words after it; or at an option login does not know and command knows or finds ambiguous (--cmd, --cf, --echo, ...). Otherwise it is a login. The mode chosen parses the whole line, so an abbreviation means what it means in that mode, and an option neither knows is refused as login's.
  4. The target: an inventory name or a literal address goes ahead with no lookup. A word one slip from a command word of four letters or more (login, command, crun, stream, daemon, config, setup, watch, version, help; one letter added, dropped, or changed, or two neighbours swapped) that is no inventory name is refused as cli_command_near_miss (exit 4): "lgoin" is not a command; did you mean login?. Any other word is looked up where its mode looks it up now: login before its credentials, command at planning, or after its credentials under daemon address authority.
  5. A shortcut's word DNS says does not exist is cli_command_unknown (exit 4): "router9" is neither a command nor a target: DNS has no such name; the registry's text widens to "neither a command nor a target". A timeout or a server failure keeps dns_timeout or dns_servfail (exit 7): the word may be a device.
  6. Unchanged: the host-key policy is the mode's, with no check of the trust store for a name DNS alone found; no lookup earlier than the mode's; nothing records that the shortcut was used, the parser handing on login or command; a stream's lines; and tab completion, which offers command words and options and never a device for the shortcut.

Accepted with it:

  • A plain word costs the configuration read and the inventory load every login makes: a broken configuration or inventory answers it with its own refusal, and a word DNS does not know waits for DNS's answer, at most name.dns-timeout.
  • A word that does not resolve leaves what karvi login WORD leaves today: an empty <ID>.id claim in the scoreboards folder, removed on a later day; for command, a job directory made and removed; with --record, the transcript of the failed session. Under daemon address authority command's credentials, a prompt among them, come before the refusal, as for karvi command WORD TEXT today; the guard keeps the mistyped command words from it.
  • A command word added later takes every device name that is a prefix of it; karvi login NAME reaches such a device.

Executed. The parser's present answers at bf009f1, through three probes of package cli given to go test -overlay, the tree untouched. A first word as the parser takes it, and a literal's address as a direct target (lines chosen from the log):

"router1"                    path=""        targets=[] cli_command_unknown
"router1 show ip int brief"  path=""        targets=[] cli_command_unknown
"c"                          path="command" targets=[] cli_device_missing
"co"                         path=""        targets=[] cli_command_ambiguous
"cr"                         path="crun"    targets=[] -
"ver"                        path="version" targets=[] -
"w"                          path="watch"   targets=[] -
"2001:db8::1"                path=""        targets=[] cli_command_unknown
"rtr*"                       path=""        targets=[] cli_command_unknown
"!r1"                        path=""        targets=[] cli_command_unknown
"login [2001:db8::1]"        path="login"   targets=[{target [2001:db8::1] true}] -
Direct("2001:db8::1") management address 2001:db8::1
Direct("fe80::1%eth0") management address fe80::1%eth0

c l r s - d j v w h and cr con lo ru se st ver he reach their commands, as does every longer prefix of a command word; co alone is ambiguous. Login's and command's option tables, every word and every prefix resolved in both:

options in both: 32, of them a different table entry: 0
login only:   --record --ssh-option
command only: --tl --cmd --cf --format --echo --border --noborder --continue-device-on-error --expect --blind --blind-return --timeout --maxbytes --blind-wait --literal --nof --of --cd --fs
words and prefixes: 291
naming two different options: 0
ambiguous in login, one option in command: 0
unknown to login, known or ambiguous in command: 96
login's meaning, refused by command:
  --e (--exclude; command: ambiguous)
  --ex (--exclude; command: ambiguous)
  --m (--management-address; command: ambiguous)
  --ma (--management-address; command: ambiguous)
  --o (--order; command: ambiguous)
  --r (--record; command: unknown)

Eleven more lines follow, the longer prefixes of --record and of --ssh-option, each unknown to command. So every option both modes take is one table entry, taking its value the same way in both, and a login reading finds the end of the options where a command reading finds it; an abbreviation's meaning changes from one mode to the other only to a refusal, never to another option. karvi r1 --e x is a login with --exclude x; karvi r1 --e x show clock is a command, refused because --e is ambiguous there (--echo, --exclude, --expect).

Found on the way.

  • README's command grammar and COMMAND-TROUBLESHOOTING's prompt entry said a karvi option may follow the command words and that -- is needed before text holding an option's name; the parser and DESIGN's freeform boundary end the options where the text begins (cmd router1 show clock --echo sends show clock --echo), and README's -- example had an unquoted | the shell would take. Both corrected in 11cf2e7, the troubleshooting entry losing its "Version 0.9.0".
  • DESIGN's section 2 shortcut entry and section 3 target set named --tl among every mode's target inputs; the table gives it to command, run, crun, and a stream's lines, not login. Corrected in bf009f1.
  • A first reading held that under daemon address authority a name only the daemon's resolver knows would refuse the shortcut. login and command run in the invoking process, and command's daemon-authority lookup is that process's own (resolver.PrepareDaemon, "the local process being the endpoint"): the resolver is the same, and the concern is withdrawn.
  • login's lookup (internal/app/login.go) takes the system resolver with no way for a test to answer in its place; command's planner takes one (planner.AddressOptions.Lookup).

Not taken.

  • A lookup before the mode's, to refuse a word that is no target before any claim: a second place that resolves, or one name looked up twice. The mode's own place leaves what karvi login WORD leaves today, and the guard keeps the mistyped command words from it.
  • Reading the line as a command first, and as a login when no command text follows: karvi r1 --echo would be refused as an option login does not know, where as a command it is refused for the text it lacks.
  • A check that a name DNS alone found has its host key in the trust store before credentials are sent.
  • An ambiguous prefix tried as a device.
  • A code of its own for a word DNS does not know: the rule is one, a first word that is a command or a target, and so is its code; dns_nxdomain, which says a target was named.
  • A bracketed IPv6 address with its brackets removed: a second spelling of one address.
  • Tab completion for the shortcut: device names at the first word, or both modes' options after a device.

Left for the build.

  • The parser: an unknown first word that is a plain name is the shortcut's, read as rule 3 says, its device a positional target marked as the shortcut's.

72. The device shortcut built (2026-10-19) #

The ROADMAP's item "A device as the first word", built by chapter 71's rule in four sections, each committed on the operator's word: the parser (005d5b6), the modes (6162641), the help and the documents (6a47cd5), and this chapter.

What it gains. karvi router1 logs in at router1 and karvi router1 show clock runs a command there, as chapter 71 agreed; a mistyped command word is refused before it becomes a connection, and a name DNS says does not exist is refused as neither a command nor a target.

Settled while building, on the operator's agreement:

  • The guard ignores case. In simple terms: a first word that matches no inventory row and is within one slip of a command word, whatever its case, is refused. Login, LGOIN, and Lgoin are refused unless the inventory names them; an inventory row matches ignoring case, so karvi LGOIN reaches the row lgoin.
  • Rule 5 kept as agreed: only DNS saying there is no such name makes the word neither a command nor a target. On a host whose resolver is systemd-resolved with no search domain, as this one, resolved does not send a one-label name to unicast DNS ("No appropriate name servers or networks for name found") and its stub answers SERVFAIL, so a mistyped one-label word there keeps dns_servfail (exit 7); a site that uses short names sets a search domain, and a word not found is then NXDOMAIN and refused, as in the container below. Not taken: SERVFAIL refused for a one-label word, which would tell an operator whose server fails that an existing device does not exist.

Where chapter 71's words left the parser a choice, it reads them literally, as reported at the first section's gate:

  • An option ambiguous in login keeps the line a login, refused as login's (karvi r1 --p x show clock: "ambiguous in login"); no word ambiguous in login is one option in command.
  • karvi r1 --record /tmp/t is login's refusal of the detached value, not a command.
  • karvi -- -r1 is a login at -r1, as karvi login -- -r1 is.
  • A blank first word stays cli_command_unknown.

74. A shorter name keeps its scratch files (2026-10-20) #

A site reported, on recorded logins, warning: transcript_timing_unreadable: /opt/karvi/shared/transcripts/261020/austin-rtr1-092239.log is rendered at 212 columns without its resizes: open /dev/shm/karvi/jsmith/karvi-script-743682-4076103593.timing: no such file or directory (the device and the operator renamed). The site starts karvi through a symbolic link, /usr/bin/k to /usr/bin/karvi: through the link every recorded login said it, and through karvi none did (the site's own check).

What it gains. A recorded login through a site's shorter name is rendered as the terminal showed it, its resizes kept; a running karvi under that name keeps its askpass socket, its ssh configuration, and its spools from another karvi's sweep. It waits on nothing.

The cause. The recording wrapper writes script(1)'s timing log into the scratch as karvi-script-<pid>-*.timing, its own pid in the name, and the login's child sweeps the scratch at its start (chapter 30). The sweep keeps a file whose pid is alive as karvi, and judged that by the base name of the pid's argv[0]: k. The wrapper was judged dead and its log removed a second into the session; at the session's end the transcript was rendered at the starting columns. The spool sweep shares the rule (osutil.KarviAlive). One other cause fits the same message: logind's RemoveIPC (chapter 57, issue 14) removes an operator's files under /dev/shm 10 s after the last logind session ends, which a recording outlives only when run outside the operator's own sessions; the site's check settled it.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms:

  • A shorter name is a symbolic link or an alias, k for the fewest keys.
  • The executable keeps its own name and place: karvi-askpass is found beside it, and the sweeps judge an owner by the name of the file it runs.
  • A pid is alive as karvi when the file it runs (/proc/PID/exe) is named karvi….

Executed. The released 0.34.0 beside a lab build of c05c432 with the change, each started as k, a symbolic link to its karvi-linux-amd64, in a 100 by 30 terminal, a fake system transport printing core1# and ending a second later, every place under the lab (link-lab.sh). The released 0.34.0:

! transcript=/dev/shm/k74/lab/released/state/transcripts/261020/core1-102258.log
! core1 [127.0.0.1] platform=generic user=lab backend=builtin-env-fallback transport=system
core1#
warning: transcript_timing_unreadable: /dev/shm/k74/lab/released/state/transcripts/261020/core1-102258.log is rendered at 100 columns without its resizes: open /dev/shm/k74/lab/released/state/tmp/karvi-script-799558-3639330774.timing: no such file or directory
! transcript=/dev/shm/k74/lab/released/state/transcripts/261020/core1-102258.log

The change's build:

! transcript=/dev/shm/k74/lab/fixed/state/transcripts/261020/core1-102300.log
! core1 [127.0.0.1] platform=generic user=lab backend=builtin-env-fallback transport=system
core1#
! transcript=/dev/shm/k74/lab/fixed/state/transcripts/261020/core1-102300.log

Both exited 0 and left the scratch empty. The lab's own script(1), the terminal the session ran in, writes a NUL at its input's end, echoed as ^@ before the second line in both runs and dropped above. While a session ran through a link kv, its wrapper's argv[0] was the link's path and its /proc/PID/exe the karvi-linux-amd64 the link names.

Why this way.

  • The file a process runs names the executable whatever link or alias started it. An upgrade that replaces the file while karvi runs leaves the kernel's /usr/bin/karvi (deleted); the suffix is dropped, as os.Executable drops it, so a karvi running across an upgrade keeps its files.
  • A renamed or copied executable is outside the rule, as it is outside karvi-askpass's: OPERATIONS says so beside the shorter name's completion.

Not taken. argv[0], what the starter chose (a link's path, or anything exec -a gives). /proc/PID/comm, which a link sets to its own name, as argv[0] (executed with a link k to bash: comm=k). The pid's start time in each file's name beside the pid: exact against a reused pid, but every name changes, and the askpass socket's longer name shortens the scratch it fits under (107 bytes in all). The timing log held open or kept anonymous: it mends the timing log alone, and the askpass socket, the ssh configuration, and the spools stay judged by argv[0]. No name check at all: a pid reused by another program would keep an abandoned file.

Found on the way. A terminal with no size, a harness with none: script(1) logs columns of -1 and the notice reads timing log line 4: columns "-1", through the link or not. A terminal an operator types in has its size; the suite's new case sizes its own.

Built. osutil.ProcessExecutableName, the base name of /proc/PID/exe without the suffix, in place of ProcessCommandName (argv[0]), and KarviAlive by it; output.SweepSpools' comment names the rule. TestProcessExecutableName; TestKarviAliveByExecutable, the test binary copied as karvi-sweep-test and run through a link k, alive, and alive once its file is removed, and the test binary under argv[0] karvi not; on the released rule it fails, a karvi started as k judged not alive. The transcript suite records a login through a link k in a sized terminal: no transcript_timing_unreadable, the start record's columns 100, the timing log gone; on the released 0.34.0 it fails at that case. DESIGN states the rule and its not-taken form, OPERATIONS the shorter name in one line, the CHANGELOG's Unreleased block the change.

Executed. gofmt, vet, go test ./... (72 packages), and make generated-clean on the final tree; all 19 suites on a lab build (run_suites, KARVI the lab build, TMPDIR=/var/tmp, 230 seconds). Under /tmp the spool suite's S9 stopped twice, in three lanes and in one, on output_preflight_space: 3,228,434,432 bytes needed, 2,757,001,216 and 2,903,162,880 free, this host's /tmp a 4.9 GB tmpfs holding 1.4 GB of other work; every suite before it passed both times. None left a /tmp/karvi-<uid>, /var/tmp/karvi-<uid>, /dev/shm/karvi, ~/.local/share/karvi, or karvi process.

75. The release 0.34.1 (2026-10-20) #

The fifteenth public release, 0.34.1, on the operator's word and number, carrying chapter 74 (a karvi started under a shorter name keeps its scratch files) and the release verifier's package folder removed at its exit (b5691fe, chapter 73's finding). At the build's start the operator set a rule for this release and every later one: the newest Go on the host and the newest version of every module. Go 1.27.3, installed on the host after 0.34.0's build, builds it (the operator: "Use the newer Go"); five modules moved, and three of karvi's uses of them needed an adaptation. No counter moves, so the daemon IPC schema stays 12 and the compatibility example is the drain, beside the released 0.34.0 daemon. The sequence is chapter 73's. It stopped twice for the operator, each time on a test that read a result before it was due on this host, and both tests were mended on the operator's word. The build stopped after the package's install check and went on to the push at the operator's second word. After publishing, the rule's check became a release tool of its own, latest.sh, the baseline's first step.

What it gains. A site has chapter 74's fix from a published, checksummed bundle and package, with the documents on GitHub Pages at the release. The native transport runs on an x/crypto with none of the ten advisories govulncheck finds on karvi's call paths at the old version, and offers mlkem768x25519-sha256 first; karvi links Go 1.27.3's fixes to crypto/x509, which the three helpers do not link. Every later release meets the rule before its build, or stops and names what is behind.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms:

  • A release builds with the newest stable Go, the first line of go.dev's VERSION; installing it on the host is the operator's (sudo bump-go.sh).
  • Every module go.mod requires moves to its newest version within its major, each move a CHANGELOG entry.
  • A new major is a new module path, a ROADMAP item (scrapligo/v2).
  • The baseline checks both first and stops before its build when one is behind.

Before the number. The archive's mirror (~/karvi/backup/archive-2026-10-19) was fetched to d7ea8db, its README noting it and its SHA256SUMS renewed; the six release tools were unchanged. A container on Docker's default network reached each address of chapter 73's probe. The baseline on a clean clone of d7ea8db passed, and was moot once the modules moved.

The three adaptations. At the new modules go test ./... failed in three packages: the native adapter, its transport, and termline. Each failure was a use of a module that the module had changed under it; the three were agreed and are in the module move's commit.

  1. A key exchange x/crypto keeps. karvi offers a name over the native transport only when x/crypto implements it, and asked x/crypto by giving SetDefaults the one name and counting one left. x/crypto now adds curve25519-sha256@libssh.org beside curve25519-sha256, so the count was two: karvi's defaults dropped curve25519-sha256, and a configured list of it alone was refused. The check now asks whether the name is among those kept.
  2. A negotiation failure by its type. karvi read a failed negotiation from x/crypto's error text with a regular expression, to name the list and both offers in ssh_algorithm_negotiation_failed. The text changed ("we offered", "peer offered"), and the failure fell through to native_session_open_failed with x/crypto's words. x/crypto now returns *ssh.AlgorithmNegotiationError, whose What names the list, RequestedAlgorithms the device's offer, and SupportedAlgorithms its own; karvi reads those, and the message is as it was.
  3. The Delete key is x/term's. karvi's line editor at a prompt translated ESC [ 3 ~ through x/term's AutoCompleteCallback into a private rune. x/term now decodes Delete itself and turns the callback off in ReadPassword, so at a password prompt the private rune went into the password: the test types secret, moves left, and presses Delete, wanting secre, and got "secre\ue000t". karvi's translation and its callback are removed.

The first stop: the heartbeat test. The baseline on a clone of 36b3ee4 failed at the release verifier's go test: TestHeartbeatRewritesTheSnapshot started a heartbeat every 20 ms and read the scoreboard snapshot once, 120 ms later. Each beat is written by atomic replacement with an fsync, free on tmpfs and costly on a disk, and the release runs with TMPDIR=/var/tmp, where the test's folder is on the root disk. The first beat, measured over 200 writers each:

TMPDIR=/dev/shm/kd/lt first beat: median 22ms, p95 22ms, p99 23ms, max 24ms, over 120ms: 0 of 200
TMPDIR=/var/tmp first beat: median 64ms, p95 125ms, p99 176ms, max 185ms, over 120ms: 11 of 200

The test now reads the snapshot every 20 ms until the first beat lands, up to 500 ms (the operator's number), and fails as before when none does (3e4af95). Operations are not touched: a beat comes every 2 s, and a scoreboard is stale only after 10 s. The baseline on a clone of 3e4af95 passed.

The second stop: the parallel-halt test. The core evidence after 1/3 failed TestParallelHalt in dispatch, unchanged since 0.34.0 and standard library only: expected unstarted: {Total:20 Terminal:20 Succeeded:19 Failed:1 NotStarted:0 Inflight:0}. Twenty tasks that take no time run two wide, the first failing, with a halt at one error; the test required some left unstarted. With more than one CPU the other worker could take and finish all nineteen while the failing task's result waited to be recorded. Failures out of 20,000 runs (the measurement's own lines):

The test as committed, go test -count=20000 -cpu N -run '^TestParallelHalt$' ./dispatch, failures:
  cpu=1 0   cpu=2 13   cpu=4 32   cpu=8 25
The test that holds every task beside a until a's failure is recorded (parallel-halt-test.patch), failures:
  cpu=1 0   cpu=2 0   cpu=4 0   cpu=8 0

A task beside the failing one now waits for the failure's recorded result (the sink's task_terminal for it), so the halt meets the rest unstarted; the test requires one failure, the halt by error count, and at most two tasks run (80f2032). Over 20,000 runs at four CPUs two had run 37 times, one the rest; with the halt's stop mutated away the test fails, a task started after the halt. The core evidence then passed.

The rule's check, latest.sh. Written after publishing, on the operator's word, from the checks the build had run by hand, and installed as the seventh release tool. release-tools/latest.sh [TREE] compares the release's Go (GO, /usr/local/go/bin/go by default) with the first line of https://go.dev/VERSION?m=text, as bump-go.sh reads it, then runs go list -m -u on every module go.mod requires, in a copy of go.mod and go.sum. Each one behind is named above its newest, and it exits 1. It also stops when it cannot check: no go.mod and go.sum, go.dev or the module proxy unread, GO unrunnable. baseline.sh runs it on the clone, into latest.txt beside the baseline's logs, and stops before the build when it fails. Not counted: a module only the graph names, a new major, and uv, ty, and ruff, which bump-uv.sh keeps and karvi does not use.

76. The operator's folder, --record=PATH (2026-10-20) #

The operator reviewed how --record=PATH applies to login. Given --record=./, karvi made a day folder in the working directory and named the files by the time, ./261020/router1-184652.log beside its metadata. The operator asked for PATH to be taken as meant, the working directory for . and ./, another path created when it does not exist; for the files to take the device's name, router1.log, with the time added only when that name is taken; and for a refusal when that name is taken too.

What it gains. A recorded login lands in the folder the operator named, under a name the operator looks for: --record=. writes router1.log where the operator stands. It waits on nothing.

The tree before. --record=PATH took the place of transcript.root alone, so the configured tree's layout came with it: PATH/YYMMDD/<device>-HHMMSS.log beside <device>-HHMMSS.meta.jsonl (the metadata's extension by transcript.metadata-format), either name taken moving both to .1, .2. The day folder serves karvi-prune, which walks the transcript trees alone and never a --record=PATH folder. README's example karvi login router1 --record=./router1.log made a folder named router1.log; Destination's comment, the refusal's text, and the suite's comment still said YYYY-MM-DD for YYMMDD.

The review. The proposal agreed, with three points raised:

  • Scope. --record=PATH alone; a bare --record keeps the day folder and <device>-HHMMSS, since prune walks day folders and a shared tree holds many sessions a day.
  • The second name carries the date. A folder without day folders spans days: with the time alone, Monday's router1-184652.log would refuse a Tuesday session started at 18:46:52. With the date, a refusal means two sessions to one device started in the same second into the same folder.
  • The pair moves together. Either name taken moves both, and each name is created exclusively, so a file of the operator's in PATH, a crun --fs=.log collection's router1.log, is never changed.

. and ./ need no case of their own: PATH is used as given.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms:

  • --record=PATH writes straight into PATH, with no day folder; PATH is created if missing.
  • Names are router1.log and router1.meta.jsonl.
  • If either is taken: router1-261020-184652.log and router1-261020-184652.meta.jsonl.
  • If either of those is taken: refused, and nothing is written.
  • A bare --record is unchanged.

The refusal, agreed with the build: transcript_name_taken, exit 111 (the output class), retryable, since a session started a second later has a free second name; the message names the folder, then ; retry, with the taken names stacked under it. transcript_path_not_directory reads --record=PATH; name a folder, its old text naming <PATH>/YYYY-MM-DD/.

Why this way.

  • An operator who names a folder means that folder, and the device's name is the one looked for; the time joins it only when the name is taken.
  • The day folder and the time in every name belong to the configured tree, which prune walks and many sessions share.
  • Each name is claimed by exclusive create, as before, so a refusal is the claim's own answer and no check races another session.

Not taken. The configured layout under PATH, the day folder and the time in every name, where the operator named the place. <device>-<HHMMSS> as the second name: the cross-day refusal. The session ID as the second name (router1-261020-184652-k3): never taken, and longer. .1, .2 after the second name: the operator chose the refusal.

Found on the way.

  • The refusal leaves the session ID's empty .id claim in the scoreboards folder, as every activity does: an activity never removes its claim, and each removes its operator's claims of earlier days, so no ID is handed out twice. PATH holds nothing of the refused session.
  • groff ends a sentence at a line ending in ., so the man page's --record=. at a line's end took two spaces after it; \& keeps one.

Built. transcript.Destination holds the root, the folder a session records into (<root>/YYMMDD, or PATH), and whether PATH chose it; Claim takes the names in order and names, under PATH, each one found taken. transcript_name_taken is registered and in ERROR-CODES. 78. The live view, --live (2026-10-25) #

While a command file per target was being settled, the operator asked when an operator sees a command session. Executed against the released 0.35.0, the answer was that the display renders each command's record once the command has completed, and a live view of the device's bytes was proposed. This session restated it for the operator's concurrence. The operator named it --live; kept it to command and run --no-daemon; made a run with it always serial, any other dispatch refused; had it follow each device's session in turn; left a daemon run to the roadmap; asked that no byte reach the terminal twice and that the session's setup be shown; and agreed the recommendations for the remaining questions. It was recorded as ROADMAP's first Next item (aa8d90b) and built in three pieces while the operator was away.

What it gains. A long command is seen as it runs: the lines of a slow show reach the screen as the device sends them, and the operator sees the login, the enable step, and the paging commands, which the text display never shows. It waits on nothing; a daemon run's live view waits in the roadmap.

The tree before. live-lab.sh, the released 0.35.0 at the fake device, whose show slow answers after four seconds, every line of standard output and standard error stamped as it arrived: standard output held nothing from 0.68 s, when show slow was sent, until 4.75 s, when its record was rendered, the running command unnamed there; the header came after the first command had completed, not at the session's open; enable and the paging commands never reached standard output, and --debug showed each step and no device byte.

The rule, agreed. In simple terms:

  • --live prints the device's bytes as they arrive, the setup included, on command, and on run and crun with --no-daemon.
  • It is display only: the records, the job's files, and the audit are unchanged, and no byte reaches the terminal twice.
  • A run with it is serial and follows each device in turn; another dispatch is refused.
  • A secret the session writes is never shown.
  • A daemon run's view is for later.

The recommendations agreed with it:

  • The bytes go to standard output in place of the text display: each device's header when its session opens, the footer after the last device, karvi's own lines as the text display prints them.
  • An exec command is shown at the prompt --echo shows.
  • Control bytes follow output.ansi.
  • --format jsonl|json, --echo, --border, and --noborder are refused beside it, and a configured border is set aside; --quiet drops the header and the footer.
  • karvi's lines are coloured, the device's bytes never.
  • dispatch.default is set to serial from --live as --ds sets it; --dispatch parallel|wave and --set of another mode are refused; the files' default yields.
  • Each secret's exact value is removed, across reads.
  • crun --no-daemon takes it as run does; a run without --no-daemon, or with --dry-run or --exercise, is refused; --nof is allowed.

Executed. live-a-lab.sh: a lab build of the working tree at the fake device (-drip 1s, -echo-secret), command router1 --live --cmd 'show clock' --cmd 'show drip' over the system transport. Every record's dispatch.mode is serial; crun's is the same, its collection line after the footer. Three refusals, karvi's standard error, each exit 4:

live_option_conflict: --live and --echo are mutually exclusive
live_option_conflict: --live without --no-daemon; add --no-daemon
live_option_conflict: --live and --dispatch parallel are mutually exclusive

Why this way.

  • Each transport reads the device's bytes in one place, so the view is given them there and nothing else changes: the records are built from the same bytes as before.
  • The plan does not carry the option, so a job and its live run hash alike, and the daemon never sees it.
  • The renderer owns standard output, so the view writes through it under its lock, and karvi's lines and the device's bytes never meet mid-line.
  • One device at a time, since two sessions' bytes interleaved would read as neither.

Not taken. The device's bytes in --debug, which carries no device output. The echo line printed when a command is sent: it names the command and shows nothing more until it completes. The bytes beside the text display: each twice. The bytes through the daemon, a frame of their own on the IPC: in ROADMAP's Later. serial written whatever the configuration says (below). The option in the plan: a display choice would change the digest.

Found on the way.

  • A site's lock refuses any write to its key, even the value it locks, so a --live that always wrote serial would be refused where a site locks dispatch.default to serial. --live writes it only when the configuration, read once beforehand, says another mode.
  • Telnet reads the device in a loop of its own, not Session.pump; it is tapped too, its password and enable secret handed to the view.
  • --follow=false on run --no-daemon discards the display; it is refused beside --live, a run with no display.
  • --li abbreviated --literal on command, run, and crun; beside --live it is ambiguous, --lit the shortest.
  • The host-key line, on standard error, comes with the device's first record, after its bytes on the screen.
  • The error-code source check refused an uncoded error in the dispatch check; it carries live_option_conflict.
  • The native suite's case numbers stop at S35, whose letters (S35a to S35f) ONLY=S35 also runs; the new case is S36.

Built. In three pieces:

  • A, command --live: platform.Live and OpenRequest.Live; devsession's pump, its exec settle loop, and writeSecret; telnet's read loop and its secret writes; platform.SecretFilter; the executor opening the view from the device's record before the transport opens, writing an exec command at its prompt, and ending the view after the driver's close; the renderer's live mode (internal/jobexec/live.go), the ping and header code shared with the text display; the option, its refusals, and live_option_conflict; the fake device's show drip (-drip, and DripGate, with which a test releases each line once the one before has been shown); a test at each layer (TestSecretFilterRemovesEachSecret, TestLiveShowsTheSessionAsItArrives, TestTelnetLiveSeesTheSession, TestLiveTakesTheTextDisplaysPlace, TestCommandLiveShowsTheSessionAsItArrives); COMMAND-SESSION's Live view.
  • B, run and crun with --no-daemon: the run's refusals, liveDispatch, TestLiveRunRefusals, TestRunLiveFollowsEachDeviceInTurn.
  • C: the native suite's S36 (command --live over both transports, a run of two devices under a parallel default, no secret anywhere, two refusals), DESIGN section 12's entry, this chapter, and ROADMAP's Next item removed, its Later item and its secrets entry updated.

(72 packages), and make generated-clean on the final tree, after each piece and at the end; all 19 suites on a lab build of it (run_suites, KARVI the lab build, TMPDIR=/var/tmp, 228 seconds), S36 among them. On the released 0.35.0, S36 fails at its first --live, cli_option_unknown: unknown option --live in command. 79. A command file per target (2026-10-25) #

ROADMAP's first Next item since chapter 78 was a folder of command files, one per target. DESIGN section 7 had settled the folder, its names (the targets' collection files'), and the refusal of a selected target without a file, and left seven questions. This session took them one at a time against a lab build of the tree at 267ec9d, in dry runs and at the fake device. The operator agreed six recommendations, replaced the fourth with a rule of the operator's own, the order as written, and asked that digests be argued from their readers rather than assumed. The design is recorded in DESIGN section 7 and was ROADMAP's Next item; its build, the next day in five sections, closes the chapter.

What it gains. One job sends each device its own list: a configuration a tool rendered per device, or checks before and after a change that differ by device, with the one job's accounting, scoreboard, dispatch, and admission. Today that is a job per device, or a stream with a --target and a --cf line for each job. It waits on nothing: the folder reader and its skips (--tf), the naming function (the collection file's), the plan's lists beside its Commands (crun's per platform), and the dry run's commands: line per target all exist.

The tree before. The labs below, a build of 267ec9d (karvi 0.35.0), LAB the scripts' name for the lab folder:

  • --cf refuses a folder, exit 4:

    commands_file_is_directory: commands file LAB/lists is a folder; --cf names one file

  • --tf given a folder reads every file in it, merged, skipping by name: of .hidden, README, disabled-nyc, nyc.txt, nyc.txt.bak, and web it read nyc.txt and web.

  • crun's dry run prints each target's list where the lists differ by platform (commands: show running-config; show version for an IOS XE device, the five Linux commands for a server).

  • --cmd values go first wherever --cf stands, and --cf is taken once (below); no operator document said so.

The rules, agreed. In simple terms:

  1. The option. --cf names a file or a folder. A file is sent to every target, as before; a folder sends each target the file named as its collection file is (core-nyc-01), read the same way. --cf - stays one list.
  2. A file that names no selected target. The targets are chosen as always (--target, --tf, --site, --all); the folder only supplies their lists. A selected target with no file is refused; a file no selected target is named for is left unread, not in the plan or the job folder. A canary is the same command with one target and the same folder.
  3. The skips and a suffix. Each target reads exactly one file, DIR/<its collection name>: lowercase, the whole name under output.crop-to-dot = false, no suffix. Nothing else in the folder is looked at, so there is no skip list. The file reads as any --cf file (empty, a folder, or unreadable: refused). Two selected targets with one name are refused, as a collection's are. --fs stays the collection's.
  4. --cmd, --cf FILE, and --cf DIR together: the order as written. Each target's list is built in the order the operator gave: a --cmd adds its command, a --cf FILE its lines, a --cf DIR that target's file; every target gets the same sequence but for what its folders supply. --cf repeats, files and folders mixed; --cf - once. A declaration attaches to the --cmd before it and goes with it into every target's list at its place. Device text stays refused beside --cmd or --cf. So --cmd="show clock" --cf DIR1 --cf DIR2 --cmd="write mem" sends each switch show clock, its DIR1 file, its DIR2 file, and write mem.
  5. The folder on crun: as on run. Commands on the line replace the platform's list, as before. karvi refuses to collect into a folder it is reading commands from, or onto a command file it is reading, on crun and on run or command with --cd or --fs. A device without its file stops the whole job at planning, a nightly crun --all included, until the tool writes a file for each device added to the inventory.
  6. The job folder's copy. It keeps what each device was sent, in a form --cf reads back: commands.txt for one list, commands.PLATFORM.txt per platform, commands/<name> per target, so karvi run --tf J/failed-devices.txt --cf J/commands reruns the failures with their own lists. A command's \r returns are written back as its trailing \r; --expect, a --blind without returns, --timeout, and --maxbytes have no form in a file, and the plan in manifest.json holds them. A command file's lines are statements, never karvi options; \r at a line's end is the one escape read, --literal turning it off.
  7. The folder as a stream line. A --cf DIR line is a --cf line like a file's: it stays from job to job until --purge-commands or --reset, takes its place in the order typed, and is read fresh at each --go.

And the digests: the plan carries each target's list and nothing is added to digest it; plan_digest already covers the whole plan; command_plan_digest only checks itself and is removed when this is built.

q7-stream-lab.sh: a stream of --target core-nyc-01.example.net, --transport native, --cf LAB/one.txt (show clock), and --go; the script waited for that job's summary to carry its final status, rewrote the file to show version, and sent --go and --end. Both jobs exited 0; the first's commands.txt held show clock, the second's show version.

The digests, by their readers. plan_digest is read by the daemon's prepare and commit (internal/daemon/client.go), the idempotency key, which refuses another plan under a committed key (internal/daemon/prepare.go), the credential package, which names its plan (internal/planner/credential.go), and the exercise report's check. command_plan_digest is read by the plan's Validate, the commit header, and the dry run's report, each comparing it with data in the same message, and shown on the dry run's commands: line; no suite, script, operator document, audit event, summary, or scoreboard reads it, and its tests check its sum.

Why this way.

  • A job is its arguments in the order given, so an operator stacks actions on one line; a folder is one more command source in that order.
  • --cf is the commands of a run, whether one list or one per target; a folder was refused, so no line that worked changes meaning.
  • The selection decides which devices run and the folder supplies their lists, as a collection folder already holds files of devices a run did not select; the refusal of a selected target without a file catches a misspelled name.
  • A lookup by exact name reads nothing else, so a skip list could only refuse a device whose own name begins with readme or disabled.
  • The names a folder shares with the collection's make the overwrite the easy mistake, so it is refused.
  • A digest earns its place by a reader that needs it; the plan's lists are covered by the one that has readers.

Not taken. A separate option for the folder: one more to learn, the same reader underneath (the cost accepted: --tf DIR merges its files, --cf DIR keeps them apart). A folder that must match the selection: a canary would need a folder of its own. --fs as the folder's suffix: on a run it turns a collection on, so typed from the folder it would write a device's output over its list. --tf's skip list. --cmd refused beside a folder, recommended first for a plan with one list per target and withdrawn: it would have dropped the operator's stacked actions, and the --cmd-first order it leaned on was the tree's departure, not the operator's rule. Every target's list written to the job folder whatever the job: a 2,500-device job with one list would write 2,500 identical files. A digest over the lists, and command_plan_digest extended to them.

Found on the way.

  • The tree sends every --cmd before a --cf file's lines wherever the --cf stands, and takes --cf once; both go with the build.
  • The job folder's commands.txt, a command file for a rerun, drops a command's \r returns and its --expect; the build writes the returns back and FILES.md says what a file cannot hold.
  • A crun can replace its own --cf file with the device's output today; the build's refusal covers a file as well as a folder.
  • internal/cli/stream.go's package comment says every job clears the commands and a command in option form is sent once; the stream's help, its kept flag, and q7-stream-lab.sh say option-form commands stay. The comment is corrected with the build.
  • command_plan_digest has no reader outside checks against its own message; it goes with the build, the plan's and the header's schemas with it.
  • A lab whose job launches the daemon stops it before removing its folder: the first run of q2-precedent-lab.sh left the daemon serving a removed folder, and it recreated an empty base/state there as it ended.

Leaves for later. A suffix on the folder's names, apart from --fs, and a job file (--jf) that carries each command's declarations, as a stream's lines do and a command file cannot: both in ROADMAP's Later. The build is ROADMAP's Next item.

Recorded. The design's evidence is kept beside the tree (release-design-evidence/cf-per-target-2026-10-25: the eight lab scripts, their logs and exits, and the answers as agreed, decisions.md).

The build (2026-10-26). Five sections, each verified and committed on the operator's word: A d07eae8, command_plan_digest removed; B 5c7ebb9, the order as written and --cf repeated; C 74e3e0c, --cf DIR; D 5a6b8f3, the collection's refusal and the job folder's copies; E, the native suite's S37 and this record. The build found nine gaps, each opened with what it gains and what it waits on, executed on the tree before it, recommended, restated in simple terms, and agreed one at a time; LAB is the scripts' name for the lab folder.

Gap B1, the scoreboard's command file beside several --cf, agreed. On the tree at d07eae8 (b1-file-lab.sh), a --cmd beside --cf LAB/one.txt gave the plan commands_file: one.txt and the scoreboard {"count":2,"file":"one.txt"}, whose one reader is the watch screen's pane line, run: 2 statements from one.txt. The rule: the plan's commands_files and the scoreboard's commands.files (scoreboard 5) name every --cf by its base name in the order given, - for standard input and a folder by its own name; the pane line joins them, run: 3 statements from one.txt, two.txt. Not taken: the first file's name alone (misleading); no field (the job's identification lost on the screen); the names joined into one string (a name may hold , ).

Gap B2, a declaration written after a --cf, agreed. b2-decl-lab.sh: the line --cmd 'copy running-config startup-config', --cf LAB/one.txt, --expect 'Destination filename.*=' exited 0, the --expect on the copy three arguments back. The rule: a declaration attaches to the command source written right before it; after a --cf it is refused, the one code for both cases, and a stream drops such a line with the same message; before every source it is declaration_before_command. The cost accepted: that line, accepted before, is refused.

declaration_with_commands_file: --expect follows --cf; write it after its --cmd (a file line takes \r at its end)

Not taken: the nearest --cmd however far back (defined, but not what the line shows); the file's last line (a file line takes no declaration).

Gap C1, a selected device without its file, agreed. On the tree at 5c7ebb9 (c1-codes-lab.sh), --cf LAB/lists was commands_file_is_directory, exit 4; a planning refusal named one device, or ten of nineteen on one line and the count left. The rule: a new code, commands_file_missing, inventory, exit 5, the folder and up to ten devices stacked, each with the file it lacks, then and N more; a device's file that exists and cannot serve takes commands_file_empty or commands_file_unreadable, exit 4, and commands_file_is_directory is retired. Built (c-folder-lab.sh):

commands_file_missing: client planning: LAB/lists has no file for 1 device
  edge-sfo-01.example.net (edge-sfo-01)

Not taken: usage, exit 4 (the folder is valid; the selection does not match it); one line joined by ; ; every device with no cap (a wrong folder under --all is 2,500 lines).

Gap C2, two selected devices with one file name, agreed. c2-collision-lab.sh: a pair whose names crop to core-nyc-01 was output_file_name_collision (exit 5) only when the run writes a text file, and accepted under --nof. The rule: a code of its own, commands_file_name_collision, inventory, exit 5, checked whenever a --cf folder is on the line and before the output's check, the remedy (output.crop-to-dot = false, or the two run apart) its description. Built:

commands_file_name_collision: client planning: LAB/lists/core-nyc-01 is the file of 2 devices
  core-nyc-01.example.net
  core-nyc-01.example.org

Not taken: output_file_name_collision widened (its name and "would both write" are wrong for an input, plainly so under --nof).

Gap C3, the lists against the IPC frame, agreed. c1-codes-lab.sh and c3-frame-lab.sh: the plan is about 900 bytes a target with one --cf file (2,500 targets 2.28 MB), and under a 1 MiB frame a run was refused ipc_frame_too_large: daemon validation: maximum 1048576 bytes, exit 112, the daemon started first and no device contacted; the client's ipc.Write refuses a request over its own daemon.max-ipc-frame-bytes. The rule: the lists stay in the plan, the frame their bound as for any plan; the refusal stacks the request's size over the bound, its description the remedy (the key, at most 64 MiB; the selection split; --no-daemon, which sends no frame); OPERATIONS gives the sizes. Built (c-frame-lab.sh), 2,500 devices of 40-line lists, refused under the 8 MiB default and accepted under 16 MiB:

ipc_frame_too_large: daemon validation: the request is over daemon.max-ipc-frame-bytes
  8957370 bytes
  8388608 allowed

Not taken: a larger default (every request may hold that much of the daemon's memory); each distinct list once (only lists devices share, which --cf FILE sends once); the lists in a transfer of their own (a new channel for a limit not met); the daemon reading the folder (it never opens an operator's file).

Gap D1, a collection over the run's own --cf lists, agreed. On the tree at 74e3e0c (d1-collect-lab.sh), crun --all --cf LAB/coll --cd=LAB/coll exited 0 with both devices' lists replaced by their output, and so did the same by a link and by crun.directory = LAB/coll with no --cd; with --fs=.txt the lists were kept and NAME.txt written beside them; run --cf LAB/coll/core-nyc-01 --cd=LAB/coll and command --cf LAB/coll/core-nyc-01.txt --cd=LAB/coll --fs=.txt replaced the file they read. The rule: a collection never writes into a --cf folder of its own run, with or without a suffix, or onto a --cf file of it, links followed; a new code, commands_file_in_collection, usage, exit 4 (the fault is two places on the line or in the configuration, the remedy another folder), at planning before the folder's lists are built; a file under no selected device's name, or under the name a suffix leaves free, and a hard link elsewhere (the collection renames a new file into place) stay accepted. Built (d-build-lab.sh):

commands_file_in_collection: client planning: a --cf folder is the collection folder
  LAB/link
  LAB/coll
commands_file_in_collection: client planning: a --cf file is the collection file of core-nyc-01.example.net
  LAB/coll/core-nyc-01
  LAB/coll/core-nyc-01

Not taken: inventory, exit 5 (the selection is not at fault); the folder refused only without a suffix (question 5 agreed both); output_file_name_collision or crun_directory_not_writable reused (the wrong subject); a warning and the run going on (the lists lost).

Gap D2, the summary's paths for the copies, agreed. d2-copies-lab.sh: one list's commands.txt dropped its file line's \r and its --cmd's --blind-return 1, and the rerun from it timed out, exit 101; crun with the platform's lists wrote commands.cisco_iosxe.txt and a --cf folder no copy, and each summary named a commands.txt that was absent; --tf J/failed-devices.txt --cf J/commands was commands_file_unreadable. The rule: the summary names only files the job wrote, commands_txt when commands.txt is written (one list for every device); commands.PLATFORM.txt and commands/ are named by rule, as output.NAME.txt is, and FILES says so. Not taken: a key per copy, or one naming the folder (nothing reads one); an empty commands.txt written always (a rerun file that sends nothing).

Gap D3, a command sent under --literal and its copy, agreed. d3-literal-lab.sh: a --literal line show clock\r was sent as written with no return, and its copy, show clock\r, reread without --literal sent show clock and one return; a --literal --cmd 'show clock' --blind-return 1 sent one return and its copy dropped it; the plan records no --literal. The rule: every copy is written for a rerun without --literal, each command its text and then one \r per return; a command whose own text ends in \r, which only --literal sends, is the one statement a copy cannot carry and reads back as returns; FILES says so, beside what a file cannot hold. Not taken: the plan recording --literal and a literal job's copies written for a --literal reread (two forms of copy, the rerun needing to know which, and such a job's returns lost); a second escape for a literal trailing \r (a grammar change for one rare case); refusing a --literal text that ends in \r (sending text as written is what --literal is for).

Gap D4, the job's audit start beside lists per platform or per device, agreed. d4-audit-lab.sh: one list's run.start carried command_count=2 and the two statements; crun with the platform's lists and a --cf folder carried command_count=0 commands=[], each device's <kind>.command events naming what it was sent; one --cf file of 4,000 lines made a 296,785-byte start event and the run was refused at its acceptance, audit_write_failed: … journald: … message too long, exit 111, as journald takes each event as one datagram (212,992 bytes on the development host). The rule: the start's command_count is the longest list's, the figure the metrics and the dry run give; commands only when every device is sent one list, and left out, not empty, beside lists per platform or per device; the audit stays 2. Not taken: every list in the start (megabytes at 2,500 devices, over the datagram bound); a platform_commands field for crun (the device events cover it, and nothing reads it); commands=[] kept (it says nothing was sent). The bound itself is ROADMAP's Later item "An audit event over journald's datagram bound", on the operator's word.

(72 packages), and the nineteen suites in 235 seconds.

81. The package update, karvi-sysutil package update (2026-10-27) #

The operator asked whether karvi updates itself: finds a newer .deb on GitHub, downloads it, verifies its checksum, and installs it; and if not, to consider it for karvi-sysutil, through curl, with -k for an internal network that inspects TLS on its way to the internet and --proxy for a proxy server. Nothing did. The session proposed the command and raised its first issue, what the checksum proves under -k. The operator made the release's signature a ROADMAP item for later, asked for the build at once with four rules of the operator's own (below), and asked what a host without the service account's daemon needs after an update.

What it gains. One root command replaces the steps of BUILD-HOWTO.md section 10 by hand (the download, sha256sum -c, apt install), from behind the proxies sites put before the internet. It waits on nothing: each release already publishes karvi_X.Y.Z_amd64.deb and its .sha256; GitHub's releases/latest redirects to the tag (302, .../releases/tag/karvi-v0.36.0), which names the version without the API; and an asset redirects once more, to release-assets.githubusercontent.com, a second host a proxy's list must allow.

The tree before. At 9c8ea43, karvi-sysutil had daemon install and daemon remove alone; ROADMAP had no item for an update; the package depends on openssh-client and adduser, not on curl.

The first issue: the checksum under -k. The .sha256 comes from the same release over the same connection as the package. Under -k anything that answers for github.com inside the network, the inspecting proxy among them, can serve another package with a checksum that matches it, and apt-get runs its maintainer scripts as root; without -k the checksum still finds only a damaged download, TLS alone vouching for the origin. The recommendation: the release signs its aggregate checksums with an SSH key, the package carries the public key, and the update verifies with ssh-keygen -Y verify (openssh-client is already a dependency). Executed with a throwaway key over 0.36.0's karvi-v0.36.0-artifacts.sha256: the file verified, exit 0; the same file with one sum changed failed, Signature verification failed: incorrect signature, exit 255. Agreed, for later: ROADMAP's "The release's signature".

The rules, agreed. In simple terms:

  1. The command. sudo karvi-sysutil package update [--check] [-k|--insecure] [--proxy URL] installs the latest release's package when it is newer than the installed one; --check only reports. A downgrade stays by hand.
  2. The refusals, before anything changes: not root; no curl (the operator's: refused, not made a dependency); a bundle install present, /usr/local/bin/karvi (the operator's: it runs before the package's, and an update would leave it in front); the package not installed.
  3. The checks. The latest tag is karvi-vX.Y.Z; the .sha256 is one line, a sum and the package's name; the package's sum is that sum. A refusal or a failure before the install changes nothing.
  4. -k covers GitHub's certificate and an https:// proxy's (the operator's): curl's --insecure and --proxy-insecure together. --proxy takes one http:// or https:// URL; a second is a usage error, since every request is HTTPS through the one proxy.
  5. Later (the operator's): the release's signature, and the update on a timer, both ROADMAP items.

The question: a host without the service account's daemon. It needs no action. An operator's own daemon (daemon.launch = "client", the default) is drained by the operator's next submission: idle, it exits at once and the client starts the installed karvi in the same invocation; holding jobs, it finishes them, killing nothing, and refuses new ones daemon_draining until it exits (OPERATIONS, "Upgrade"). Under daemon.launch = "systemd", the service account's daemon or each operator's where a site's global file locks it so, an instance keeps its program and its account's submissions are refused daemon_incompatible until systemctl restart, which lets the jobs finish within daemon.shutdown-grace-seconds and cancels what remains. So the update lists the active instances of karvi-daemon@*.service and names each one's restart, and on a jump box prints nothing more. In simple terms: the update never restarts a daemon; an operator's own daemon needs nothing, the next run switching it over; each running instance under systemd is named with its restart, whose moment stays the administrator's, as the package's postinst has it (chapter 57, issue 16). Agreed; whether an unattended update restarts is the timer item's question.

Executed. In a throwaway ubuntu:26.04 with curl and no network, the lab package karvi_0.36.0+dev_amd64.deb (a make build of the tree over 9c8ea43 with the update) installed, tools/release-fixture serving a release karvi-v0.37.0, the lab package repacked at that version, and KARVI_RELEASES naming the fixture:

# karvi-sysutil package update --check
karvi-sysutil: cannot reach https://127.0.0.1:8443/releases/latest; nothing changed
curl: (60) SSL certificate OpenSSL verify result: self-signed certificate (18)
exit 1
# karvi-sysutil package update --check -k --proxy https://127.0.0.1:8445
package  karvi 0.36.0+dev
latest   karvi 0.37.0
newer    sudo karvi-sysutil package update installs it
exit 0
# karvi-sysutil package update -k --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8444
package  karvi 0.36.0+dev
latest   karvi 0.37.0
fetched  karvi_0.37.0_amd64.deb  6542362 bytes
checked  karvi_0.37.0_amd64.deb  sha256 as its .sha256
updated  karvi 0.36.0+dev to 0.37.0
exit 0
# karvi-sysutil package update -k
package  karvi 0.37.0
latest   karvi 0.37.0
current  no newer release
exit 0
# karvi-sysutil package update --proxy 192.0.2.10:2025
karvi-sysutil: --proxy takes an http:// or https:// URL
  given 192.0.2.10:2025
exit 2

The fixture's log showed the --check through tls-proxy CONNECT 127.0.0.1:8443 and the update's three requests each through proxy CONNECT. scripts/sysutil-smoke-test.sh's new step 10 runs the same under systemd with the service account's daemon running, and two refusals in the bundle's step 13; on the lab package it passed, every step:

  • the refusals, each exit 1 with the accounts and karvi's places as before: not root, no curl, a bundle's karvi beside the package, a certificate not trusted, the proxy's not trusted, a checksum of zeros, a tag v2, an asset missing; and, in step 13, the package not installed and the bundle's own install;
  • --proxy given a socks5:// URL, and given twice, exit 2;
  • an older release, 0.1.0, current under -k;
  • the fixture's origin certificate trusted through update-ca-certificates: --check without -k reports the newer 99.0.0; through the HTTPS proxy without -k refused, with -k reported;
  • the update through the HTTP proxy without -k: the package at 99.0.0, karvi-sysutil: karvi-daemon@karvi.service keeps the karvi it started with; systemctl restart karvi-daemon@karvi.service, the daemon's pid the same, the work folder gone; and again, current.

Why this way.

  • The redirect, not the API: no JSON for a bash script to read, and no rate limit of 60 an hour per address, which every host behind one proxy shares.
  • apt-get install of the file, not dpkg -i: a new dependency comes with it. The work folder is opened to 0755 so that apt's sandbox user _apt reads the package.
  • curl --disable: root's .curlrc cannot turn verification off unseen. curl's https_proxy and no_proxy from the environment still apply, which sudo drops unless its policy keeps them, so --proxy is the option.
  • --proto =https and --proto-redir =https: no request or redirect leaves HTTPS; an http:// proxy still carries the tunnel.
  • curl's first error line alone: curl 8.18 follows a certificate error with several lines of advice.
  • KARVI_RELEASES: the test's server, and a site's mirror in GitHub's layout.

Not taken. The GitHub API (above). A signed apt repository on gh-pages: apt and unattended-upgrades would carry the proxy, -k (Acquire::https::Verify-Peer), and the schedule, at the cost of the hosting, a key in apt's keyring, the pruning of each release's 6.5 MB, and the restart still outside apt. curl in Depends or Recommends (the refusal names it). --cacert FILE: a host trusts an inspecting authority through update-ca-certificates, as the test does. The instances restarted after the install. An update under the bundle: a newer bundle's install.sh is that install's update.

Found on the way.

  • A development package, 0.36.0+dev, sorts after 0.36.0, so a lab install sees the release as current; the tag check takes X.Y.Z alone, as a release's tag is.
  • An update makes three requests, each its own tunnel through the proxy: the redirect, the package, and its checksum.

Built. Over 9c8ea43, committed in two on the operator's word, the feature and then ROADMAP's items: packaging/sbin/karvi-sysutil (package update, the usage, refuse taking an exit status); packaging/man/karvi-sysutil.8; tools/release-fixture, the test's releases and proxies; scripts/sysutil-smoke-test.sh (curl in the image, step 10, two refusals in step 13); CHANGELOG.md's Unreleased; OPERATIONS "Upgrade" and the service account's "After an upgrade"; BUILD-HOWTO.md section 10; DESIGN section 8; and FILES' row for karvi-sysutil; then ROADMAP's two Later items.

The evidence is kept beside the tree (update-design-evidence/: the container test's log, the transcript and the script and image that made it, and the signature lab).

82. The native transport without scrapligo (2026-10-27) #

ROADMAP's Next 1, opened on the operator's word. The scrapligo-v1 adapter is a wrapper and nothing more: it passes karvi's own x/crypto/ssh connection to scrapligo as a custom transport (transport.NewTransport, WithCustomTransport), and scrapligo's Read, Write, and Close hand the bytes back. The device session, the host-key policy, system, and Telnet are karvi's own code. Designed in this session, one gap at a time, and recorded for the build; the program is unchanged.

What it gains. No scrapligo move with each of its releases: the module, its pins in the verifiers, the help text, karvi version, the evidence file, and a full battery run, over code karvi never runs (0.36.0's move was a NETCONF change). Three modules leave vendor/ (scrapligo, gotextfsm, and creack/pty, 139 files), and about 18 KB of scrapligo code the executable. The release checks that exist only for scrapligo go: the import boundary, the version pins, release/SCRAPLIGO-EVIDENCE.md, and BUILD-QUALIFICATION's rule that the version output names ScrapliGo. Nothing an operator runs is lost. It waits on nothing, and lands before scrapligo's next release would have to be taken. The cost is a breaking configuration change: scrapligo-v1 is named in 65 files outside vendor/.

The gaps, in the order taken: what ssh.transports still means; the new implementation ID; the package and file names; the retired error codes' text; what replaces the evidence and the release requirements; and ROADMAP's ScrapliGo v2 item.

Gap 1, ssh.transports, agreed. In simple terms: ssh.transports keeps what still chooses a program, the OpenSSH executable and the exec: slots; what could only ever name the one native implementation goes.

  1. Kept: ssh.transports.system, an executable path, and a custom slot NAME = "exec:PATH", another OpenSSH-compatible program.
  2. Removed, and refused at load: the key ssh.transports.native; a custom slot's builtin:ID or bare ID value; an implementation ID given as a mode's selector; and the selector preferred.
  3. native stays the selector's name wherever an operator writes one: --transport native, the inventory's transport column, and ssh.<mode>.transport.
  4. The implementation ID is then seen only where gap 2 finds it.

Checked while recording: a removed key moves the registry, from 31 to 32, and leaves the configuration schema at 6, as 0.31.0's removal of output.files.summary-json moved the registry from 29 to 30 alone.

Not taken: keeping ssh.transports.native with one legal value, a key whose only valid setting is its default; removing ssh.transports whole, when system and the exec: slots still choose a program.

Executed. The released 0.36.0 (bin/karvi; the tree's Go code is unchanged since), with a lab configuration in /dev/shm, removed after:

$ karvi config show ssh.transports.native

exit 2
$ karvi config validate c2.toml       # alt = "exec:/usr/bin/ssh", native2 = "builtin:scrapligo-v1"
valid: true
$ karvi config validate d.toml        # ssh.command.transport = "scrapligo-v1"
valid: true

karvi version lists scrapligo: 1.4.3 (id=scrapligo-v1, linkage=compiled-in) under ssh_transports:.

Gap 2, the implementation ID, agreed. In simple terms: no new ID; the native transport is called native, as system and telnet are called by their names.

  1. Selection.Implementation goes: with every transport's ID its kind, it repeats Kind, which is used in its place.
  2. karvi version lists native: compiled-in over system: external-executable; the JSON keeps its shape, with "id": "native", and the job manifest's copy with it.
  3. The words: login's refusal, "transport native is not system-compatible SSH"; the exercise finding, "native transport available" (and "system transport available", today "system transport system available"); the --debug line without implementation=.
  4. No record changes: a command record already carries the kind, and a login record system or telnet alone, login refusing native.

Checked in the build: whether the job schema (5) moves for the manifest's changed value.

Not taken: a new ID such as karvi-v1, one more word with only one value; x-crypto, a library the version output does not list.

Executed. The released 0.36.0 against the fake IOS XE device (cmd/karvi-fake-device built from the tree), with a lab in /dev/shm, removed after. After gap 1 the ID is seen in four places, and in no record:

command --transport native   → record "transport":"native"
command --transport system   → record "transport":"system"

The fourth is run --exercise's finding, native transport scrapligo-v1 available (internal/jobexec/exercise.go), from its format %s transport %s available over the kind and the ID.

Gap 3, the package and file names, agreed. In simple terms: one package, internal/transport/native, laid out like systemssh and telnet.

  1. The adapter's dial.go and exec.go, with their tests, move into internal/transport/native. The connection is the devsession.Stream itself; scrapligo's wrapper, its logger, and the stream shim go.
  2. provider_scrapligov1.go becomes native.go; scrapligoDriver becomes driver, and openScrapliGoV1 becomes open.
  3. The registry goes, one implementation always compiled in: register, Available, the map of openers, and Factory.Implementation. Admits keeps its platform list.
  4. internal/buildinfo/transport_scrapligov1.go goes, with the registration; karvi version's two entries are a fixed list.
  5. internal/adapters/ keeps sshkey alone.

Not taken: renaming the adapter (internal/adapters/xcryptossh) and keeping two packages, whose one reason, the scrapligo import boundary, is gone.

Executed. go list on the tree at 293b1df:

internal/transport/native: 2 files        (registry.go, provider_scrapligov1.go)
internal/transport/systemssh: 6 files     (driver and connection in one package)

internal/transport/native     -> internal/adapters/scrapligov1   (its only importer)

The adapter is karvi's own x/crypto/ssh connection (the dial, the host-key policy in the handshake, the keepalive, the authentication, and exec), passed through scrapligo's Transport and read back by stream.

Gap 4, the error codes, agreed. In simple terms: the text names the native transport where it says what holds now, and keeps scrapligo where it is the history; two codes retire, and one new code refuses an ssh.transports entry that cannot be used.

  1. The active session_keepalive_timeout says "native-ssh.keepalive-* on the native transport".
  2. The retired codes keep scrapligo where it is what the code was about, and name the native transport where they say what holds now: host_key_scan_failed, "...; the native transport checks the key in its own handshake"; native_command_failed, "...; karvi's device session now runs its commands"; native_driver_create_failed and native_platform_create_failed, "..., which the native transport no longer uses". native_response_nil is unchanged, history and still true.
  3. Runtime messages naming the ID follow gap 2: ssh_algorithms_unavailable's "which scrapligo-v1 cannot use" names native; the native_session_open_failed lines about scrapligo's logger and transport go with the wrapper.
  4. Retired: native_transport_unavailable, the native transport in every executable; transport_implementation_invalid, no implementation IDs.
  5. New: transport_mapping_invalid refuses at load an ssh.transports entry whose value is not exec:PATH (system's, an executable path), or that takes a built-in transport's name, native or telnet.
  6. transport_custom_slot_default says "which only the system slot accepts".
  7. preferred and scrapligo-v1 as selectors need no code: they are ordinary slot names, transport_mapping_missing when no slot maps them.

Checked: the registry artifact carries the active config_* codes alone (errorcodes.ActiveWithPrefix("config_")), so the transport_* codes do not move it; gap 1's key moves it.

Not taken: a row for ssh.transports.native in the removed-keys table (internal/configload/removed.go), the removals since 0.31.0 being plain unknown keys and this one a slot's name, not a registered key; keeping the name transport_implementation_invalid, a word gap 2 removes.

  • DESIGN's mangen entry named run's build-dependent help, gone in section 1.
